items.title: Ethiopia Calls for Shift from Climate Commitments to Action Ahead of COP32

original_payload.original_title: Ethiopia Calls for Shift from Climate Commitments to Action Ahead of COP32
original_payload.original_body:
Addis Ababa, November 14, 2026 (ENA)— Ethiopia has called for a stronger focus on translating global climate commitments into concrete action through enhanced financing, investment and international partnerships.
Minister of Finance and COP32 Chief Negotiator Fitsum Assefa has also emphasized the need to bridge the gap between climate ambitions and implementation, particularly in developing countries during a series of high-level engagements at COP31 in Antalya, Türkiye.
Speaking at a high-level event on financing the implementation of Nationally Determined Contributions (NDCs) through the Climate Promise Forward initiative, she highlighted the importance of integrating climate priorities into national budgets, investment frameworks and financing strategies.
She noted that finance ministries have a critical role in translating climate commitments into practical development interventions by aligning climate objectives with national economic priorities and mobilizing the resources required for implementation.
Fitsum further stressed the need to strengthen cooperation among governments, development partners and financial institutions to ensure that climate plans generate investment opportunities and tangible results.
During discussions about advancing the Baku-to-Belém Roadmap, the Minister emphasized the importance of translating global climate finance ambitions into practical support that addresses the financing needs of developing countries.
She highlighted the need for affordable and appropriate financing, stronger institutional capacity and more effective delivery mechanisms to ensure that developing countries can implement their climate commitments.
The Minister underscored the importance of international partnerships in closing the gap between climate plans and implementation while exchanging perspectives with global philanthropy leaders at a roundtable hosted at the Ethiopia Pavilion.
Meanwhile, at the launch of the Climate Implementation Bridge (BRIDGE), a COP31 Presidency legacy initiative designed to help countries translate climate commitments into investable projects, Fitsum stressed the importance of connecting national climate and development priorities with financing, investment and technical support.
The initiative has brought together participating countries, the United Nations Development Programme and multilateral development banks to strengthen cooperation and advance the implementation of climate commitments.
The engagements reflect Ethiopia's emphasis on connecting climate finance, national development priorities and international partnerships as it prepares to lead the global climate process through the COP32 Presidency.
Through its upcoming presidency, Ethiopia is seeking to advance an implementation-oriented climate agenda that connects global commitments with financing and tangible outcomes on the ground.

items.title: Ligue Nationale : Le National Dendi arrache le nul face à Zumunta FC dans les dernières minutes

original_payload.original_title: Ligue Nationale : Le National Dendi arrache le nul face à Zumunta FC dans les dernières minutes
original_payload.original_body:
Dosso, 14 novembre (ANP) – Le National Dendi de Gaya et le Zumunta FC de Niamey se sont neutralisés sur le score d’un but partout (1-1), ce samedi 14 novembre au stade régional de Dosso, à l’occasion de la 5ᵉ journée du championnat de la ligue nationale, le championnat de la première division de football au Niger.
Cette rencontre opposait deux formations ambitieuses qui abordaient cette journée avec respectivement 7 points pour le National Dendi et 6 points pour Zumunta FC après les quatre premières journées du championnat.
Dès les premières minutes, les deux équipes ont affiché leurs intentions offensives dans une rencontre caractérisée par un engagement physique et tactique de haut niveau. Ce sont finalement les visiteurs qui ont ouvert le score à la 18ᵉ minute grâce à leur milieu de terrain Yacouba Oumarou, dossard numéro 8, qui a trompé la vigilance de la défense du Dendi pour donner l’avantage au Zumunta FC.
Malgré plusieurs offensives des locaux, le score est resté inchangé jusqu’à la pause, permettant au club de la capitale de rejoindre les vestiaires avec une avance d’un but.
Au retour des vestiaires, le National Dendi a accentué la pression sur son adversaire. Multipliant les assauts et les changements tactiques, les joueurs de Dendi ont fini par être récompensés de leurs efforts à la 89ᵉ minute lorsque Nassouridine Nouridine, portant le dossard numéro 9, a inscrit un magnifique but d’égalisation, soulevant l’enthousiasme des supporters présents au stade régional de Dosso.
À l’issue de la partie, l’entraîneur principal du Zumunta FC, Jacques André, a félicité les deux équipes pour leur prestation.
« On a assisté à un match vraiment costaud. Les deux équipes se sont battues corps et âme et à la fin on s’est retrouvé avec un match nul. Ce sont deux équipes qu’il faut suivre, qui sont vraiment en train de faire tout pour retrouver la Super Ligue. C’était vraiment une rencontre intense », a-t-il déclaré.
Le technicien a également annoncé que son prochain rendez-vous sera face à Zongorzo FC de Maradi à Niamey.
Pour sa part, l’entraîneur du National Dendi, Abdramane Garba, a souligné l’intensité de la rencontre et l’impact de ses choix tactiques.
« Le match a été d’une intensité très élevée. Heureusement que les enfants ont eu les ressources nécessaires pour revenir au score. Nous avons encaissé un but à la 18ᵉ minute et cela a mis beaucoup de pression sur l’équipe. Il fallait attaquer tout en défendant. C’est pourquoi j’ai effectué trois changements dès la reprise puis un quatrième changement qui a permis d’obtenir l’égalisation », a-t-il expliqué.
Évoquant la suite de la compétition, le technicien du Dendi a indiqué que son équipe se déplacera à Niamey pour affronter le RCL lors de la prochaine journée.
« Notre objectif est d’aller le plus loin possible et d’atteindre le niveau auquel aspirent tous les clubs. Incha Allah, nous comptons faire mieux lors des prochaines sorties », a-t-il affirmé.
Grâce à cette égalisation obtenue dans les ultimes instants de la rencontre, le National Dendi conserve son invincibilité à domicile et maintient ses ambitions dans la course aux premières places, tandis que Zumunta FC repart de Dosso avec un précieux point à l’extérieur.
AMM/KPM/ANP-111Novembre 2026

items.title: Lancement à Agadez de la 2ème phase de la Caravane nationale de sensibilisation et de mobilisation générale

original_payload.original_title: Lancement à Agadez de la 2ème phase de la Caravane nationale de sensibilisation et de mobilisation générale
original_payload.original_body:
Agadez, 14 novembre 2026 (ANP) – Le Secrétaire Général du Gouvernorat d’Agadez, M. Souleymane Saïdou Boulhassan a présidé, ce samedi 14 novembre 2026, la cérémonie de lancement de la deuxième phase de la Caravane nationale de sensibilisation et de mobilisation générale.
Cette caravane a pour thème central : « Civils et FDS : main dans la main contre les menaces des ennemis du Niger ».
Pour le secrétaire général du gouvernorat d’Agadez, « le Niger consolide chaque jour sa sécurité et son intégrité territoriale, et ce, en parfaite synergie avec les pays frères de l’Alliance des États du Sahel (AES) ».
Il a salué et félicité le groupe Yan Maza Na Tigre, le Chœur de la Garde nationale du Niger, ainsi que l’ensemble du comité d’organisation pour cette initiative citoyenne d’envergure nationale.
Rappelant le parcours de la caravane, M. Souleymane Saïdou Boulhassan a ensuite informé qu’« après avoir sillonné avec succès les régions de Diffa, Zinder, Maradi et Dosso lors de la première phase, vous avez entamé cette deuxième phase à Tillabéri. Aujourd’hui, vous marquez votre empreinte à Agadez, avant de poursuivre votre périple vers Tahoua et Niamey ».
Selon lui, « à travers la musique, la culture, les conférences et les séances de sensibilisation, vous accomplissez une mission essentielle : rapprocher davantage les populations civiles de leurs Forces de défense et de sécurité et perpétuez la mémoire de nos héros ».
M. Souleymane Saïdou Boulhassan a ensuite fait observer que « la région d’Agadez, par sa position géographique stratégique et l’immensité de son territoire, constitue un verrou vital pour la sécurité nationale et sous-régionale ».
Il a salué le travail remarquable accompli par les Forces de défense et de sécurité qui œuvrent jour et nuit, souvent dans des conditions difficiles, pour protéger les personnes et leurs biens.
Il a, à cette occasion, exprimé la gratitude de l’État et de l’ensemble de la nation à l’endroit de ces forces.
S’adressant aux populations d’Agadez, le secrétaire général du gouvernorat a rappelé que « la sécurité n’est pas l’affaire des seuls hommes en uniforme, elle est un devoir collectif ».
Le fait est que, a-t-il dit, « face aux menaces multiformes et aux tentatives de division, notre bouclier le plus solide demeure la franche collaboration entre les civils et les FDS. Soyons vigilants, cultivons la cohésion sociale, rejetons les rumeurs et soutenons sans réserve nos forces engagées sur le terrain ».
Intervenant à son tour, l’administrateur délégué de la commune urbaine d’Agadez, le chef de bataillon Assarid Almoustapha a souligné l’importance de cette caravane, qui vise, selon lui, à renforcer la cohésion sociale et la sécurité.
Il a invité les populations à écouter attentivement les messages qui seront délivrés, à rester vigilantes et à dénoncer tout comportement suspect.
Le chef de bataillon Assarid Almoustapha a également fait remarquer que « dans le contexte actuel de la refondation de notre pays, sous la conduite du général d’armée Abdourahamane Tiani, Président du Conseil national pour la sauvegarde de la patrie et Chef de l’État, la mobilisation générale n’est plus un slogan, mais un devoir patriotique ».
Pour sa part, le président du comité d’organisation, M. Nafiou Salissou, il a déclaré : « Le groupe Yan Maza Na Tigre et le Chœur de la Garde nationale saluent, avec déférence et un respect indéfectible, la vision éclairée, la fermeté et le patriotisme de nos dirigeants, avec à leur tête Son Excellence le Général d’armée Abdourahamane Tiani, Président du Conseil national pour la sauvegarde de la patrie, Chef de l’État et son excellence Monsieur le Premier Ministre Ali Mahamane Lamine Zeine, ainsi qu’à l’ensemble de l’équipe gouvernementale, pour leur engagement en faveur de la refondation de l’État, de la protection de l’intégrité territoriale et de la promotion de la justice sociale ».
« Sous leur conduite inspirée, le Niger avance fièrement vers son émancipation totale », a-t-il ajouté.
M. Nafiou Salissou a souligné que cette dynamique patriotique trouve ses racines dans le succès retentissant de la première phase, qui a conduit la caravane de Diffa à Dosso, en passant par Zinder et Maradi.
« Après avoir lancé notre deuxième phase à Tillabéri, nous sommes aujourd’hui dans l’Aïr pour dire que le nord du Niger, dans toute sa diversité, se dresse comme un seul homme », a-t-il déclaré.
Il a enfin exprimé sa gratitude aux Forces de défense et de sécurité, soulignant que « leur sacrifice quotidien au milieu des rigueurs du désert permet à notre pays de tenir bon ».
La cérémonie a été marquée par des prestations musicales assurées par les troupes des Forces de défense et de sécurité.
NAK/KPM/ANP-110 Novembre 2026

items.title: Nigeria's upcoming election marred by rising AI disinformation

original_payload.original_title: Nigeria's upcoming election marred by rising AI disinformation
original_payload.original_body:
Politics   Nigeria
Nigeria's upcoming election marred by rising AI disinformation
Abiodun Jamiu
11/14/2026  November 14, 2026    As Nigeria inches closer to the 2027 polls, the use of artificial intelligence in the electoral process has prompted questions about integrity and institutional readiness. Can Nigerians trust their democratic processes?
https://p.dw.com/p/5PRq5
Prefer DW on Google
Nigeria's 2027 general election will take place against the backdrop of AI-driven disinformation Image: Adekunle Ajayi/NurPhoto/picture alliance       Advertisement
Nigeria  has just over two months to go until its general election, with incumbent  Bola Tinubu  running on a ticket focused on combating  raging insecurity  and resolving the nation's  economic crisis . He faces off against former Vice President Atiku Abubakar and senior opposition figure Peter Obi.
The country's electoral body, the Independent National Electoral Commission (INEC), recently released its preliminary voter's register, which reportedly is riddled with images believed to have been generated using  artificial intelligence (AI) .
Among the telltale signs of AI usage were exaggerated facial features in images and inconsistencies on the electoral registers, such as duplicates of names and even identities of people who since the previous election had died.
The development raises concerns about the body's overall preparedness ahead of the country's upcoming 2027 general election. Instead of making the upcoming vote more transparent by allowing access to its procedures, INEC has come under fire amid broader controversies about the expanding influence of AI in elections across the continent.
Is Nigeria becoming a one-party state?
To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that  supports HTML5 video
Fake news: Nothing new in Nigeria
Joash Amupitan, the chairman of the electoral commission, said the body is now investigating the development, focusing on discrepancies potentially created by AI use.
To this end, he announced the establishment of a dedicated unit to monitor AI-related threats, detect deepfakes and strengthen the integrity of the electoral process, warning that the credibility of the upcoming election could otherwise be under attack.
Supporters of a particular candidate in the election can be easily manipulated to believe AI-driven fake news Image: Sani Maikatanga/AP Photo/picture alliance
However, even prior to the  proliferation of AI across Africa  and the globe, this would not be the first time that Nigeria has found itself in the unfortunate position of having to deal with the circulation of  fabricated images , doctored audio and fake videos online. In the run-up to the  2023 election , deepfakes falsely linking candidates to terror-related activities filled social media platforms.
These are often designed to promote certain candidates or to discredit opponents in a bid to influence public perception, which now with the use of AI could create disinformation campaigns of new proportions.
Artificial intelligence has various effects on voter behavior
Lois Ugbede, the assistant editor at the factchecking platform DUBAWA, told DW that "based on our monitoring so far, AI-driven disinformation is serious and is becoming commonplace."
"This could influence political discourse and voter behavior ahead of 2027 because we are already seeing parties using inflated crowds to show that they have a large followership or support," she added.
Have some elections become an empty ritual?
To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that  supports HTML5 video
At the same time, rather than influencing the vote in favor of any particular candidate, "the deeper danger is that people may begin to doubt authentic information simply because they know convincing AI-generated fakes are possible," said Akintunde Babatunde, executive director of the Abuja-based Centre for Journalism, Innovation and Development.
"We often focus on the risk of people believing an AI-generated falsehood, but there is another problem where genuine evidence can be dismissed as AI-generated," he noted, citing instances of a lawmaker who recently made inflammatory remarks during a campaign rally — but then claimed the clips were manipulated.
Further pitfalls behind a lack of safeguards against AI
Chibuike Mgbeahuruike, an election consultant at the Centre for Democracy and Development, told DW that apart from the spread of synthetic content online, AI intrusion into the electoral commission's portal could also "undermine its institutional credibility, especially with the low level of confidence that we are already witnessing."
He added, however, that AI itself is not inherently a threat to electoral integrity. The real threat lies in "the absence of effective accountability for its deployment," as innovations in tech increasingly appear to infiltrate governments and their democratic processes.
"Voters must have confidence … that the technology is also transparent, accountable and independently scrutinized, and ultimately subject to human and institutional oversight," said Mgbeahuruike.
Journalists can be just as susceptible to disinformation created by AI and other technologies Image: Emmanuel Osodi/AA/picture alliance
Mallam Jibrin Baba Ndace, the director-general of state-owned broadcaster Voice of Nigeria, agrees, urging journalists at a recent conference also to not fall into the trap of believing reports, which later could turn out to be false due to AI manipulation.
He stressed the importance of  protection measures and due diligence  in news media, with the growing inability of public institutions like INEC to provide impartial information due to the use and influence of AI and other election-related tech.
Nigeria's marred relationship with new tech
Beyond AI, Nigeria's electoral processes have undergone various  technological shifts  over the years in hopes of improving transparency while increasing efficiency.
Electoral authorities first deployed electronic assistance in 2011, when Direct Data Capture Machines were introduced; the devices collect voters' biometrics by scanning fingerprints or capturing facial recognition data with webcams to stop voters from submitting multiple ballots.
Ten years later, a system called the Bimodal Voter Accreditation System (BVAS) was introduced as the new standard, designed to combine fingerprints with facial recognition. However, during the 2023 general election, this voting process was marred by system failures, as poor cell signals delayed these voter accreditation procedures.
Nigeria's voting procedures have increasingly been digitalized since 2011 Image: Pius Utomi Ekpei/AFP
However, with INEC tallying more than 103 million Nigerians registered to participate in the coming poll, disinformation, fake news and technological challenges amount to only a few of several concerns pertaining to Nigeria's democracy.
Voter apathy has become a particular concern, especially among the country's youth. The 2023 election recorded the lowest voter turnout since the country's return to democratic rule in 1999, with merely 27% of registered voters going to the polls.
Abiodun Jamiu   Nigerian freelance multimedia journalist.          @Real_Abiodun01

items.title: South Sudan pushes back elections amid violent flare-ups

original_payload.original_title: South Sudan pushes back elections amid violent flare-ups
original_payload.original_body:
Politics   South Sudan
South Sudan pushes back elections amid violent flare-ups
Wesley Dockery   with AFP, AP, Reuters, dpa
11/14/2026  November 14, 2026    South Sudan has been independent from Sudan since 2011, and has not yet held national elections. Since then, the country faces cycles of violence after a civil war led to a tenuous peace deal.
https://p.dw.com/p/5PSY2
Prefer DW on Google
The Republic of South Sudan is Africa's youngest country (FILE: November 15, 2016) Image: Justin Lynch/AP Photo/picture alliance       Advertisement
South Sudan  on Saturday pushed back its first national elections from December to February next year, as the country faces flare-ups of violence and political strife.
Why were the elections pushed back?
Presidential and legislative elections  are now slated for February 11, 2027.
"We didn't postpone the elections. We have just adjusted the time to allow other processes to be implemented and that is according to the law," National Elections Commission spokeswoman and Commissioner Josephine Achiro said.
"Article 57 of the National Elections Commission gives us authority to adjust the elections timelines," she added.
Achiro said the postponement of the election date is for voter registration and civic education purposes.
According to the World Bank, the vast majority of South Sudanese lack state-recognized ID, creating challenges for voter registration. Thousands of centers have been established across the country to register voters.
What is the political situation in South Sudan?
South Sudan became independent from  Sudan  in July 2011 following a referendum. The country has some 12 million people and is one of the impoverished nations on the planet.
From 2013 to 2018, forces backed by President Silva Kiir, a member of the Dinka ethnic group, fought against troops supported by Vice President Riek Machar, who hails from the Nuer tribe. More than 400,000 people died in that conflict.
A fragile peace agreement was achieved between the two sides in 2018, with a national unity government established in 2020.
South Sudanese President Salva Kiir (right in photo) and Vice President Riek Machar are the country's two most prominent political figures and belong to two different ethnic groups (FILE: September 10, 2019) Image: Denis Elamu/Photoshot/picture alliance
Kiir dissolved South Sudan's transitional government in September ahead of elections, and has since ruled by decree in a caretaker administration. He fired Vice President Machar, who had earlier been charged with treason and is under house arrest.
Despite the peace deal, there are also frequent clashes between the Dinka and Nuer groups loyal to Kiir and Machar.
Growing violence
The head of the UN Mission in South Sudan, Anita Kiki Ghebo, said earlier in the week that  violence is increasing and added that approximately 10 million people in South Sudan need some form of humanitarian assistance. She also noted that 1.4 million people have entered South Sudan due to an ongoing  conflict in Sudan .
"If left unaddressed, political, security, and humanitarian challenges risk reinforcing one another, further exacerbating tensions adn vulnerabilities across the country," she said.
She has urged renewed dialogue "to focus on establishing clear and credible roadmap for completing the outstanding provisions of the Revitalized Peace Agreement," the formal name for the 2018 peace deal.
Wesley Dockery   Journalist and editor focused on global security, politics, business and music.

original_payload.original_title: ICPC to publish recovered assets, owners, status
original_payload.original_body:
THE Independent Corrupt Practices and Other Related Offences Commission (ICPC) has pledged to periodically publish recovered assets, their status and owners, to promote transparency and accountability.
Hassan Mohamed, Chairman, Local Organising Committee (LOC) of the maiden General Assembly of the African Asset Recovery Practitioners’ Forum (AARP-F), gave the assurance during a pre-conference media briefing in Abuja on Saturday.
Mohamed, also Director of Special Services at ICPC, said nothing concerning recovered assets was hidden, emphasising that the information would remain accessible to the public.
The assurance comes as 54 countries prepare to converge on Abuja to discuss strategies for preventing the loss of billions of dollars through corruption and illicit financial flows.
He spoke during a question-and-answer session ahead of the assembly, scheduled to hold from November 17 to November 20 in Abuja.

items.title: Patrimoine foncier : La sécurisation des terres à vocation agricole au cœur d’un atelier à Abomey

original_payload.original_title: Patrimoine foncier : La sécurisation des terres à vocation agricole au cœur d’un atelier à Abomey
original_payload.original_body:
Le Ministère de l’Agriculture, de l’Élevage et de la Pêche (MAEP) et le Ministère de la Décentralisation et de la Gouvernance Locale (MDGL) ont organisé, conjointement, le vendredi 13 novembre 2026 à Abomey, un atelier de sensibilisation des Préfets sur la mobilisation et la protection des terres rurales à vocation agricole pour les projets d’investissement. Les travaux, présidés par les deux ministres, ont réuni l’ensemble des Préfets autour de la préoccupation majeure liée à la sécurisation des terres à vocation agricole.
En effet, ces terres sont sous la menace permanente de disparition en raison de l’urbanisation galopante. « Les terres cultivables sont passées de 43 % en 2021 à 41 % en 2023, soit 2 % de terres agricoles perdues en deux ans », a expliqué Antoine HOUEDJI, le Conseiller technique aux affaires foncières du Ministre de l’Agriculture, de l’Élevage et de la Pêche. Cet état des lieux appelle à des actions concertées pour la sécurisation du patrimoine foncier. D’où cet atelier, qui a permis d’exposer la problématique aux Préfets et d’en appeler à leur implication.
Les différentes communications ont porté, entre autres, sur la pression foncière et ses conséquences, le cadre juridique de protection du foncier agricole, les rôles des maires et des préfets, ainsi que la cartographie, la délimitation et le cadastre, et les opportunités d'investissement communal.
« Dans le cadre de la stratégie Bénin Vert 2033, nous voulons également identifier et sécuriser, dans chaque commune, une réserve foncière de plusieurs hectares pour mettre en œuvre l’initiative "Une commune, un poumon vert" », a révélé Monsieur Adin Yéton BLOUKOUNON GOUBALAN, Ministre de l’Agriculture, de l’Élevage et de la Pêche.
À son collègue de la Décentralisation, Monsieur Janvier YAHOUEDEHOU, d’insister sur la responsabilité collective de protéger aujourd’hui les terres dont notre pays aura besoin demain : « Protéger nos terres agricoles, c’est préserver notre souveraineté alimentaire, soutenir le développement de nos territoires et préparer l’avenir ». « Notre rôle est décisif pour intensifier, mobiliser et sécuriser les réserves foncières à vocation agricole », a affirmé Laurent ZOMAÏ, Préfet du département du Zou.
Une séance du même genre aura lieu bientôt avec les maires des 77 communes que compte le Bénin. Ce faisant, le Gouvernement entend renforcer la gouvernance foncière et garantir une meilleure protection des terres rurales à vocation agricole.

items.title: INTERVIEW EXCLUSIVE : Le Prophète Malachie invoque la justice divine pour porter Juliana Lumumba à l’OIF

original_payload.original_title: INTERVIEW EXCLUSIVE : Le Prophète Malachie invoque la justice divine pour porter Juliana Lumumba à l’OIF
original_payload.original_body:
Alors que le huis clos électif du prochain Sommet de la Francophonie au Cambodge approche à grands pas, la course au Secrétariat général de l’OIF se joue aussi sur le terrain invisible. En marge des festivités de son 4e jubilé sacerdotal célébré à la paroisse Temidiri Ilara Imeko, à la frontière du Bénin et du Nigeria, le Prophète Malachie (Église des Chérubins et des Séraphins) a officiellement placé la candidature de Madame Juliana Lumumba Amato sous un puissant « bouclier spirituel ». Dans cet entretien exclusif, le leader spirituel lève le voile sur cette alliance mystique internationale, invoque la mémoire des ancêtres et rappelle pourquoi la fille de Patrice Lumumba est portée par un destin biblique face aux coalitions diplomatiques terrestres.
Prophète Malachie, vous venez de célébrer votre 4e jubilé sacerdotal à la paroisse Temidiri Ilara Imeko, à la frontière du Bénin et du Nigeria. À cette occasion, vous avez posé un acte fort en plaçant la candidature de Madame Juliana Lumumba Amato au Secrétariat général de l’OIF sous un « bouclier spirituel ». Pourquoi une église chrétienne s’implique-t-elle si ouvertement dans une élection géopolitique ?
Prophète Malachie : Soyons clairs : rien de ce qui se passe sur la scène visible du monde ne s’accomplit sans avoir été préalablement scellé dans l’invisible. La politique et la diplomatie ne dérogent pas à cette règle divine. L’Église des Chérubins et des Séraphins est une église de révélation et de combat spirituel. Lorsque le Seigneur nous montre qu’une cause est juste et qu’elle porte en elle les germes de la paix et de la dignité pour notre continent, nous ne pouvons pas rester les bras croisés. Le livre des Proverbes nous rappelle d’ailleurs : « Quand les justes se multiplient, le peuple est dans la joie ; quand le méchant domine, le peuple gémit » (Proverbes 29:2). Le parrainage que nous offrons à Madame Juliana Lumumba Amato n’est pas un choix partisan, c’est une mission divine de protection et d’élévation pour l’Afrique au sein de la Francophonie.
Vous parlez de « bouclier spirituel ». En quoi consiste concrètement ce déployement à l’approche du Sommet de Phnom Penh au Cambodge ?
Prophète Malachie : Un bouclier sert à parer les flèches. Dans ces instances internationales, les enjeux sont colossaux, les rivalités intenses, et les pressions mystiques ou humaines sont réelles. Durant les trois jours de rassemblement avec les hauts dignitaires et les leaders spirituels du Bénin et du Nigeria, nous avons érigé des remparts de prières. Nous avons invoqué les forces célestes pour lui accorder la clarté d’esprit, la faveur des dirigeants qui voteront à huis clos, et pour briser tous les verrous spirituels qui se dresseraient sur sa route. « Quand la terre africaine s’accorde dans le secret de la prière, aucun décret des hommes ne peut altérer la marche du destin. » Nous appliquons la promesse de l’Écriture : « Car tu bénis le juste, ô Éternel ! Tu l’entoures de ta grâce comme d’un bouclier » (Psaume 5:12). Nous préparons le terrain invisible pour que sa victoire soit une évidence dans le visible à Phnom Penh.
Au cours des célébrations, vous avez mis un point d’honneur à honorer la mémoire des défunts. Quel lien faites-vous entre le culte des ancêtres et la fille du héros national congolais, Patrice Emery Lumumba ?
Prophète Malachie : Les racines d’un arbre déterminent la force de ses branches. Le sang d’un martyr comme Patrice Lumumba crie encore pour la justice et la souveraineté de l’Afrique. Juliana Lumumba porte en elle cet héritage mémoriel lourd et noble. Prier pour les âmes disparues, c’est libérer les bénédictions de demain et apaiser l’histoire. Sa vision d’une « Francophonie des peuples » passe précisément par l’apaisement des mémoires blessées de notre espace francophone. Comme le veut la sagesse de notre terroir : « L’arbre ne s’élève vers le ciel qu’en puisant sa force dans la terre où dorment les ancêtres. » La Bible elle-même déclare que « la mémoire du juste est en bénédiction » (Proverbes 10:7). En honorant la mémoire de ceux qui ont tout donné, nous connectons sa mission terrestre à une lignée de dignité. Elle ne marche pas seule ; elle est portée par l’histoire.
Le programme de Juliana Lumumba, « Neuf projets neufs pour une Francophonie neuve », fait face à une concurrence féroce, notamment celle de la Secrétaire générale sortante, Louise Mushikiwabo, soutenue par le Rwanda. Le combat spirituel peut-il faire pencher la balance face à de telles puissances diplomatiques ?
Prophète Malachie : Les coalitions humaines et les alliances diplomatiques faillissent là où la volonté de Dieu s’impose. Certains dirigeants s’imaginent qu’un sommet international se gère avec des valises de billets et des promesses de couloir, mais ils oublient que le Tout-Puissant ne prend pas de commissions et ne valide pas les faux rapports. Le programme de Madame Lumumba, axé sur la jeunesse, l’intelligence artificielle et surtout une Académie francophone de la paix, répond aux besoins profonds des peuples, et non à des calculs de corridors. Les tensions géopolitiques actuelles exigent un leadership de réconciliation. Le Bénin et le Nigeria, à travers notre voix, envoient un signal : l’Afrique de l’Ouest et l’Afrique Centrale s’unissent par l’esprit. L’adage de chez nous nous enseigne bien que « l’eau a beau bouillir, elle n’oublie jamais qu’elle vient de la source ». Les verrous sauteront un à un, car ce projet puise sa légitimité à la source même des aspirations africaines. Rappelons-nous ce que dit l’Éternel des armées : « Ce n’est ni par la puissance ni par la force, mais c’est par mon Esprit » (Zacharie 4:6). Cela dépasse de loin les calculs des hommes.
Un dernier mot pour les fidèles et pour la candidate à quelques semaines du verdict ?
Prophète Malachie : Aux fidèles, je demande de maintenir la flamme de l’intercession. À Madame Juliana Lumumba Amato, je dis : soyez sans crainte. Le bouclier est déployé, l’alliance mystique est scellée sur cette terre frontalière bénino-nigériane. Que votre cœur soit fort, car la couronne de la Francophonie cherche une tête digne, et l’esprit a déjà choisi la direction de la paix.
Que tout le monde s’en souvienne : nous, les serviteurs de Dieu, nous ne sommes rien d’autre que des esclaves de Dieu. Nous n’exécutons que ses ordres sacrés et sa sainte volonté. C’est pourquoi j’aime rappeler ce proverbe de nos anciens : « L’esclave qui marche avec courage sous les ordres du Roi ne craint jamais la fureur de la tempête. » Notre Roi, c’est le Tout-Puissant, et Sa tempête balaiera les obstacles sur le chemin de notre sœur.

items.title: Was it lawful to delay South Sudan’s elections until February 2027?

original_payload.original_title: Was it lawful to delay South Sudan’s elections until February 2027?
original_payload.original_body:
South Sudan’s Parliament was dissolved for a December election. The vote has moved to February, and Parliament remains dissolved. On 22 September 2026, President Salva Kiir dissolved both houses of the Transitional National Legislature and installed a caretaker administration. The general elections were then three months away. On 14 November, the National Elections Commission (NEC) announced that polling would move from 22 December 2026 to 11 February 2027. The Commission said it needed more time to distribute voter registration materials and complete other preparations. That explains why it wanted more time. The legal power to postpone the elections nationwide remains unidentified in its reported explanation.
The authorities gain 51 days to prepare. The country is left with 11 days between polling and the agreed end of the transition on 22 February 2027. In the meantime, voters have less time than the law guarantees to check the register, and candidates face compressed deadlines for qualifying and campaigning. What law authorises the Commission to move the vote nationwide? Do voters have the time they are guaranteed to check the register and correct mistakes? Do candidates have time to qualify and campaign on equal terms? What keeps Parliament dissolved now that polling has moved? Who may govern, and who will hold them to account, if the handover runs past 22 February? The answer at each stage affects what can lawfully happen at the next.
In my view, the legal foundation of the caretaker government is void because of the way the 2026 reforms were adopted. The peace agreement can be amended only through the procedure it prescribes. Article 8.4 requires the consent of at least two-thirds of the Council of Ministers and at least two-thirds of the voting members of the Reconstituted Joint Monitoring and Evaluation Commission (RJMEC). The amendment then goes to the Transitional National Legislature for ratification under the constitutional amendment procedure. The sequence matters. Consent must come before ratification. A condition imposed at the start of the process has to be met at that stage. Articles 8.2 and 8.3, which were reportedly retained, give the agreement priority where it conflicts with the Constitution or ordinary legislation. Article 3 of the Transitional Constitution, in turn, gives the Constitution priority over inconsistent legislation.
The 2024 extension shows how the procedure works. The parties agreed to extend the transition to 22 February 2027. RJMEC gave its consent, and the legislature then ratified the extension. In July 2026, the legislature approved changes that would allow elections before a national census and a permanent constitution. Constitutional Amendment No 13 and the amendments to the Elections Act followed in September. The latter supplied the stated basis for the dissolution. RJMEC says the July changes reached the legislature without the consent of its voting members required by Article 8.4.
RJMEC speaks to whether its own members gave that consent. Its account is decisive in assessing whether the required procedure was followed. Ratification is the last step. A vote in the legislature cannot supply the consent that should have come before it. In my view, the July amendments therefore failed to take effect, and the earlier provisions of the agreement continue to govern wherever they conflict with the 2026 reforms. Those reforms are inconsistent with the surviving provisions of the agreement and with the Transitional Constitution that incorporates it. One such provision, Article 1.1.4, ties the unity government’s mandate to the transition and to the holding of elections, subject to the agreement’s exceptions. RJMEC considers the unilateral dismantling of the Presidency inconsistent with that article. The caretaker administration rests on the 2026 reforms. The defects in those reforms therefore go to the very foundation of the caretaker administration.
There is a second argument, which proceeds on the government’s own premises. Assume for the moment that the reforms were valid. The Commission would still have to show that the Elections Act authorised what it did. Lawyers call this arguing in the alternative. The starting position concerns whether lawful authority existed at all. The alternative asks whether, assuming the claimed foundation was valid, the authorities exercised their powers lawfully. The first position stands as the second is tested. A public body may exercise only the powers the law gives it. When its authority is challenged, it must identify the source of that power and show that it met the conditions for using it. That is the burden the authorities must discharge here. On the public record, their explanation leaves those questions unanswered.
The Commission’s power to move the vote
Moving an election date fixed by law requires authority for the change, compliance with the conditions attached to that authority and proper notice. Any power the NEC relies on must also be exercised within the limits of the Constitution. The calendar presents the first difficulty. Section 9(1) of the National Elections Act, 2012, as amended in September 2026, directs the NEC to organise elections in December 2026. The same subsection places polling within the final 60 days of the transition, reflecting the 60-day lead time set by the Revitalised Agreement on the Resolution of the Conflict in the Republic of South Sudan. Published accounts of Constitutional Amendment No 13 describe amended Article 197A(9) as retaining both the December mandate and the 60-day requirement.
The Commission could make a plausible point about the arithmetic. Counting back 60 calendar days from 22 February puts the start of the window on 24 December. The original polling date of 22 December falls two days before that window appears to open. The proposed February date falls within the window. But section 9(1) also says December. A reading that allows a February election would give effect to one part of the subsection by defeating the other. The mismatch points to poor drafting. It gives the Commission no discretion to choose which part of the subsection to follow. A reading that can sustain the February date must account for both requirements. If the published accounts reflect the operative text of Amendment No 13, Article 3 also makes the constitutional December mandate binding, however broadly the Commission reads the Act.
Any power to depart from the date must cover the elections in question, and the NEC must meet its conditions. The Act lets the Commission postpone elections for President, governor or chief administrator by notice if proven imminent danger makes voting impossible or if a state of emergency has been declared for the territory affected. It must then choose the earliest practicable date, no more than 60 days after the original one. There is also a narrower power for returning officers, with the Commission’s approval, to defer polling in particular geographical constituencies.
The 51-day delay fits the outer limit. That is the one condition the reported timetable can show it meets. The Commission’s reported explanation concerns registration logistics and gives no finding of impossibility due to imminent danger or an applicable emergency declaration. If insecurity is the basis, the NEC must identify where it made voting impossible and explain why the delay had to be nationwide. Even if it could do that, the specific power covers only the three executive offices named in the Act. The returning officers’ power is local. A nationwide postponement of all legislative elections needs a separate source of authority, and none has been identified.
The Commission could fall back on its ordinary scheduling authority and on section 138. That section allows the NEC to adapt procedures when a mistake, an emergency or another specified circumstance makes the existing rules unsuitable. It requires the Commission to inform political parties and independent candidates of the action it takes. It expressly puts the Constitution outside the reach of that power. And reading it to allow a nationwide change of date would let the Commission use a general power to evade the specific conditions the Act sets for postponement. It would also deprive the December mandate of effect. The specific rule governs postponement where it applies. Section 138 gives the Commission a general power to adapt procedures within those limits.
Then there is notice. Section 16(1) ordinarily requires at least six months’ notice of polling. The announcement on 22 June met that interval for the December election. The NEC announced the February date 89 days before polling. A valid postponement notice might carry the original notice forward. That depends on the Commission first showing that it could lawfully postpone the polls. As a fresh notice, the 14 November announcement falls about three months short of the ordinary rule.
These are four tests for the same decision. The December mandate stands in the way of a February poll. The specific postponement power is limited in scope, and compliance with its conditions has yet to be shown. The general power cannot override those limits or the Constitution. The June notice can carry forward only if the postponement was valid. The need for more time may be real. The Commission still has to show where the law gives it the authority to move the vote.
What the timetable takes from voters and candidates
For a voter, the effect of the revised calendar starts with the register. Article 26 of the Transitional Constitution protects the right to vote, which depends in practice on whether the voter is correctly registered. Section 36(e) of the Act requires publication of the register at least three months before polling so voters can check their entries. Section 37(c) requires the Commission to open it for inspection within 60 days of the general election notice and to keep it open for at least 15 days. Section 38(1), which the 2026 amendment does not expressly revise, requires publication of the final register at least six months before polling. These periods protect the accuracy of the register. The law sets them so that voters can spot errors in time to do something about them.
Registration was due to begin on 14 November. The provisional register is scheduled for publication on 29 November. Radio Tamazuj and Eye Radio give different dates for the display of the register. Each reports a seven-day display period, with final publication scheduled for early January. For an 11 February poll, the three-month deadline fell on 11 November, three days before registration was due to start. Publication on 29 November is 18 days late. If the June notice still governs, the 60 days allowed for opening inspection have long expired. Whatever notice applies, seven days is less than half the required 15. The final register misses the six-month deadline and would also miss the three-month deadline if the newer provision were read to govern both registers.
South Sudanese legal expert Dr. Remember Miamingi
Consider a voter displaced by conflict who discovers that her name is missing or that she has been registered in the wrong constituency. The inspection period is her opportunity to have the error corrected. Shortening it leaves voters most exposed to mistakes with less time to put them right. The NEC has identified no power that permits it to shorten these minimum periods and has given no explanation of how it will protect voters who miss the shortened window. On the present record, the timetable cuts a statutory safeguard for the right to vote without demonstrated legal authority.
The same register determines whose endorsement counts for a candidate. Article 26 protects the right to stand as well as the right to vote. Section 48(1) requires a presidential candidate to obtain the support of 10,000 registered voters from at least seven states, with at least 200 from each. Section 48(3) requires the NEC to issue forms for collecting signatures for presidential and gubernatorial nominations 30 days in advance. The 15-day rule in section 70(4), as amended in 2026, applies to forms for geographical-constituency seats. Section 49(2) requires the nomination period for candidates for President, governor and chief administrator to open at least 60 days before polling. The Act also addresses the campaign. Sections 75(1) and 75(3) require publication of the final legislative candidate lists after appeals and simultaneous announcement of a campaign of at least 30 days. Section 80(1), as amended, caps the overall campaign at 45 days. Sections 81 and 82 require impartial treatment of candidates and require the Commission to regulate equal access to public media.
The timetable provides for signature forms to be issued on 29 November, applications to open on 14 December and nominations to close before publication of the final register. It sets 18 January for the final candidate lists and schedules campaigning from 27 December to 9 February. If the dates for forms and applications apply to the presidential and gubernatorial races, those candidates have 15 days to collect signatures, half the 30 days the Act gives them. The opening on 14 December is 59 days before polling, one day short of the section 49(2) minimum. And because nominations close before the final register appears, candidates must obtain endorsements from registered voters without a final register against which to check them. The Commission has yet to say how candidates can verify signatures or how it will treat endorsements from voters whose details are corrected on appeal.
The overall 45-day campaign fits the cap. A legislative candidate whose name appears on the final list on 18 January after a successful appeal would have at most 23 calendar days to campaign, counting that day. The statutory minimum is 30. Campaigning begins while nomination appeals can still change who is allowed to stand. Candidates who succeed on appeal bear the greatest disadvantage because they join the contest last. Even an equal allocation of public airtime after publication of the final lists would leave them with fewer days to reach voters. Impartial treatment has to be secured over the campaign as a whole, including for candidates who needed an appeal to get on the ballot.
The signature, nomination, verification and campaign stages depend on one another. The timetable gives candidates less time to collect signatures before nominations open late. They must then file before the final register lets them check those signatures, and candidates admitted on appeal stand to lose part of their campaign. Each shortfall feeds the next. The Commission has offered no legal basis for compressing the statutory periods. The effect on the right to stand is the same as the effect on the right to vote. The timetable takes away time the law set aside to make each right meaningful.
Governing without Parliament
The postponement also extends the period in which South Sudan is governed without a national legislature. Sections 16(2a), 16(2b) and 16(4b) of the amended Act tie the dissolution of the legislatures, the partial dissolution of the national government and the removal of the vice-presidents to the three months before polling. Those powers may be exercised only within that window. The September order fell at the start of it under the December timetable. If the February date stands, the country will have been without a national legislature for nearly five months before voting. RJMEC’s objection under Article 1.1.4 remains. The agreement ties the unity government’s mandate to the transition and the holding of elections, subject to its own exceptions.
The government can argue that the order was lawful when it was issued because it fell within the three months before the December election. That assumes the validity of the reforms, which my primary argument disputes. Even on the government’s reading, the order’s original timing answers only whether the statutory window applied then. The window was tied to polling, and polling has moved. A new date does not by itself reconvene Parliament. The September order continues to operate unless a competent authority sets it aside or otherwise provides for the legislature. Its continuing operation and its continuing legality are separate questions. The longer the dissolution lasts beyond the period used to justify it, the harder it is to identify a legal basis for it and the sharper the conflict with Article 1.1.4 becomes.
No authority has explained what keeps the dissolution lawful for the extra seven weeks. The postponement stretches an arrangement framed around three months before polling and leaves the country without the institution that could supply the missing legislative authority.
The next question is who can hold power after 22 February and who can hold them to account. Section 16(4a) keeps the incumbent President in office during the electoral period until the elected President takes over. Published accounts of Constitutional Amendment No 13 also describe a constitutional basis for continuity in the presidency pending succession. The Act separately provides for temporary continuity in the executive offices covered by its specific postponement power, where that power is lawfully exercised. It allows up to 60 days after polling for a presidential run-off. Article 86(5) of the Transitional Constitution bars the President from making provisional orders on matters affecting general elections. Continuity in office is one issue. Authority to extend the transition and arrangements for legislative oversight each require a legal basis of their own.
The reported calendar provides for first-round results on 15 February, a possible run-off by 12 April and disputes through 15 July. An outright winner could take office before the transition ends. A run-off after 22 February or a court order suspending a result could push the handover past that date. The dispute period running through July does not itself suspend a result. The timing of a possible run-off is the clearest way to see how much the postponement changes the prospects for an orderly handover. With December polling, the 60-day period would have ended on 20 February, before the transition expired. With February polling, it runs to 12 April, seven weeks beyond the agreed end of the transition. The revised calendar therefore creates a risk of a presidential run-off after expiry of the transition that the original calendar avoided.
For as long as the caretaker administration is in place, the September order restricts substantial public borrowing and other major commitments unless the President authorises them and the applicable law allows them. Both houses remain dissolved. This leaves the executive to supervise its own caretakers within those limits. Parliament cannot scrutinise spending or summon ministers to account for it. The continuity provisions can keep an incumbent in office. They confer no power to prolong the mandates of the wider transitional institutions or restore parliamentary scrutiny. Article 86(5) also places provisional presidential law-making on general elections outside the available remedies. A decree cannot lawfully cure the defects in the timetable.
This is a question of accountability now. Power is already being exercised without the legislature that would ordinarily check it. The authorities have yet to explain on what legal basis, within what limits and under whose oversight that power could be exercised after 22 February. Whatever continuity means for the office of the President, the country still needs answers about the rest of the transitional government and the absence of parliamentary oversight.
The five questions lead to a single conclusion. Without a valid power to postpone, the February date has no lawful footing. A date with no lawful footing cannot justify taking time away from voters and candidates. With Parliament dissolved, the body that could supply the missing legislative authority cannot act. And unless the transition is lawfully extended, a handover after 22 February leaves the wider exercise of power without a clear legal basis. The Commission’s explanation that it needs more time answers none of these points.
That conclusion follows even on the assumption that the 2026 reforms are valid. My primary conclusion also stands. The caretaker government rests on amendments adopted without the consent required by the peace agreement. More careful use of the powers claimed under those reforms cannot cure that defect at the foundation. On either reading, the February timetable cannot be lawfully defended on the basis the authorities have offered.
If a South Sudanese court sets aside the presidential or parliamentary results on these grounds, or a regional court with jurisdiction orders relief that requires them to be set aside, South Sudan could find itself beyond 22 February 2027 with no valid electoral mandate for the offices affected and Parliament still dissolved. Restoring legislative oversight or extending the transition would require separate legal authority. The Elections Act provides for a rerun without fresh nominations, so a second vote could carry forward the very exclusions that made the first vulnerable to challenge. Rival claims to govern could deepen divisions among the parties to the peace agreement, put the ceasefire under further strain and expose civilians to renewed violence.
The writer, Dr. Remember Miamingi, is a South Sudanese expert in governance and human rights, as well as a political commentator. He can be contacted via email at  remember.miamingi@gmail.com

items.title: Voter registration begins in Eastern Equatoria amid logistical gaps

original_payload.original_title: Voter registration begins in Eastern Equatoria amid logistical gaps
original_payload.original_body:
Electoral authorities in Eastern Equatoria State have begun voter registration in the state capital, Torit, but logistical delays and difficulties reaching remote communities could hamper efforts to register eligible voters across the state.
The exercise was launched at Nyong Primary Health Care Centre in Torit, with authorities planning to establish 460 registration centres across the state’s 11 geographical constituencies.
However, registration materials had not yet reached all designated centres, while the deployment of election officials was still underway, raising concerns about the pace of the rollout.
Oryema Emmanuel, deputy chairperson of the Eastern Equatoria State Election High Committee, said all registration materials were available at the state level but would be distributed to individual centres in phases.
“All the materials for registration are available at the state level now,” Emmanuel said.
He said authorities planned to deploy about 3,220 registration officials across the state but did not provide a timeline for completing the deployment.
Emmanuel said mobile registration teams would be sent to remote villages, cattle camps and other hard-to-reach areas to enable residents to register.
“Those categories of people will be handled by mobile registration teams,” he said.
He did not specify how many mobile teams would be deployed or when they would begin operating.
Access concerns
Civil society organisations warned that long distances to registration centres, limited public awareness and difficulties obtaining identification documents could prevent some eligible citizens from participating.
Wodcan Lazarous Saviour, executive director of SPIDO, said civil society groups had a responsibility to provide accurate information and counter misinformation and hate speech during the electoral process.
He said the distance to registration centres could discourage participation, particularly among residents of remote communities.
“If people have to travel long distances to reach these registration centres, some of them may end up not participating in the registration process,” Saviour said.
He also questioned whether citizens without national identity cards would have equal opportunities to register.
Emmanuel said applicants would be expected to present a South Sudanese national identity card, passport or other supporting documents to establish their citizenship. Local identification officers familiar with residents in their communities would help identify eligible applicants who lacked formal identification documents, he added.
Saviour urged authorities to ensure that the process is accessible to all eligible citizens and that no one faces intimidation or discrimination because of their ethnic or religious background.
“No one should be intimidated, and no one should be mistreated because of tribe, religion or any other differences,” he said.
South Sudan’s general elections are scheduled for Feb. 11, 2027, after repeated postponements. The elections will be the country’s first since it gained independence in 2011.
original_payload.original_summary: Electoral authorities in Eastern Equatoria State have begun voter registration in the state capital, Torit, The post Voter registration begins in Eastern Equatoria amid logistical gaps appeared first on Radio Tamazuj .

items.title: US envoy Kushner says he aims to broker Europe-Russia talks on Ukraine

original_payload.original_title: US envoy Kushner says he aims to broker Europe-Russia talks on Ukraine
original_payload.original_body:
US envoy Jared Kushner has said he is working with Russia, Ukraine and Europe to move peace talks to the next stage, including facilitating direct engagement between Europe and Moscow.
Kushner told reporters Saturday that “both sides” know that compromises will be necessary to end the war, and that he and fellow envoy Steve Witkoff were now working on next steps.
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items    list 1 of 3  Trump-Xi-Putin trilateral meeting at APEC: What to expect
list 2 of 3  Russian casualties ‘reach 450,000’: What that means for the Ukraine war
list 3 of 3  US suggested Ukraine cede parts of Donbas to Russia to become part of NATO
end of list
Trump son-in-law’s comments follow peace talks in Abu Dhabi on Tuesday that failed to reach a breakthrough on ending the war, but resulted in a  prisoner exchange .
The prospect of Europe’s involvement in the talks has grown in recent weeks, with leaders  agreeing on Friday  to send five representatives of European countries to represent the bloc at future peace talks.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said on Wednesday he did not think it was possible to think about European security “without Europe”.
The Kremlin has signalled an openness to negotiations with Europe, but it has criticised a lack of proposals from the bloc.
The five countries attending are the United Kingdom, France, Germany, Italy, and Poland – the five countries that have signalled readiness to send troops as part of a “coalition of the willing” to secure Ukraine in the event of a ceasefire.
In a lengthy post on X on Saturday, French President Emmanuel Macron said that the bloc must “state clearly” what it wants for the post-war period, “including to the Russians”.
Macron also stated his belief that Ukraine, which has Europe’s largest conventional army, has a key role to play in Europe’s post-war context alongside NATO, which he added is a “place where it fully belongs”.

items.title: More than 100,000 rally across France in new Yellow Vest protests

original_payload.original_title: More than 100,000 rally across France in new Yellow Vest protests
original_payload.original_body:
More than 100,000 people have taken to the streets in France in another round of cost-of-living rallies organised by the “Yellow Vests” and various youth movements.
Saturday’s protests saw a decline in turnout compared with previous weekends and stayed largely calm, authorities said.
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items    list 1 of 3  Police clash with protesters as anti-government rallies sweep France
list 2 of 3  Mapping how France’s protest wave spread across Europe
list 3 of 3  France accelerates minimum wage hike in bid to quell protest
end of list
The Ministry of the Interior reported that 106,000 people took part in protests nationwide, including 24,000 in Paris – down from 146,000 people nationwide and 46,000 in Paris last week. Student unions place Saturday’s protest numbers higher, at 200,000 people, including almost 100,000 in the capital.
The country has been gripped by high-school blockades, mass demonstrations, and strikes for more than a month, with protesters rallying against falling educational standards, cost-of-living increases, low wages, and police violence.
A number of demonstrators also carried signs targeting President Emmanuel Macron, who has faced significant criticism from protesters.
Some rallies in recent weeks have seen violence at the fringes, and the first major protest on October 17 saw looting in cities across France. Since then, police presence at rallies and controls on transport and permits to protest have been expanded.
Marseille, France’s second-largest city, banned protests over the weekend, but the prefecture announced that some 3,500 people still took to the streets. Local media reported that tear gas and a water cannon were used against protesters and shared images of fires burning in a popular local square.
In Lyon, local media reported that roughly 8,000 people took to the streets. They shared images of masked protesters chanting in front of fires lit in the street and police charging and using tear gas.

items.title: Tens of thousands march in latest Portugal housing protests

original_payload.original_title: Tens of thousands march in latest Portugal housing protests
original_payload.original_body:
Tens of thousands of people have taken to the streets of more than 30 towns and cities in Portugal to protest against surging rental prices, demanding urgent government action to address the country’s worsening housing crisis.
Organised by the Casa Para Viver (A Home to Live In) platform, demonstrations on Saturday took place under the slogan “They will not steal our right to a home,” with protests in Lisbon, Porto, Faro, Portimao, Coimbra, Braga and other locations. It was the biggest national demonstration  since the social movement began weeks ago .
Recommended Stories
list of 4 items    list 1 of 4  How has the cost of living changed in France, Italy, Spain and Portugal?
list 2 of 4  Portugal cost-of-living protesters pour back into camps cleared by police
list 3 of 4  Portuguese police clear Lisbon housing protest camp, arrest 25
list 4 of 4  Police storm Portugal housing protest camp
end of list
Participants, ranging from teenagers to retired people, walked behind large banners, with the Lisbon march punctuated by drums, music, and chanting. Protesters called for caps to be placed on rent increases, greater legal protection for tenants against eviction, and more affordable housing. They also demanded the reversal of proposed changes to rental legislation.
One woman on a protest march in Lisbon told Al Jazeera that she was a business owner, “and I can’t afford a house.”
“I can’t say much more than this. I’m forty-years-old, I can’t go to a bank and just buy a house with my money,” she added.
Another woman told Al Jazeera that she had joined the march to protest “for a better life, for all of us, not just the young people, all of us, because we deserve to have a home.”
One man told Al Jazeera “we have been suffering this for the last three or four years, and I have many friends and family in this situation, they had to move because they cannot afford the rent. If you earn, for example, a thousand euros, and you have to pay rent of six hundred, seven hundred, then you cannot live, it’s impossible.”

items.title: Pope Leo urges end to violence in Peru during visit to remote Andes town

original_payload.original_title: Pope Leo urges end to violence in Peru during visit to remote Andes town
original_payload.original_body:
Pope Leo XIV has called for an end to the violence gripping Peru, urging people not to respond to injustice with brutality, as he visited  communities he once served as bishop.
“We feel threatened by the uncertainty of widespread violence and by the unspeakable suffering that continues to afflict so many of our brothers and sisters, he said, speaking at his former cathedral in Chiclayo.
Recommended Stories
list of 4 items    list 1 of 4  Pope Leo meets clergy abuse survivors in Peru amid calls for justice
list 2 of 4  Pope Leo XIV warns on pressures facing modern families
list 3 of 4  Pope thanks crowds on emotional return to ‘second home’ in Peru’s Chiclayo
list 4 of 4  Pope Leo cheered on return to Peru city where he served as bishop
end of list
Peru’s homicide rate has nearly doubled over the past five years, from 5.8 to 10.7 per 100,000 people. Reported extortion cases rose from 2,421 in 2019 to 26,734 in 2025, according to official figures cited by The Associated Press.
Security was a top concern for Peruvians in the last election. Conservative President Keiko Jujimori  took office in July  after promising to tackle crime. She has since declared states of emergency, including in Lima in August, then in September in prisons holding inmates linked to criminal organisations.
She has also pursued closer ties with Washington,  bringing Peru into the ‘Shield of the Americas,’  a US-led regional coalition formed to carry out joint military operations against drug cartels.
Later on Saturday, in the Andean town of Santa Cruz de Succhabamba with a population of about 6,000, about 20,000 people came to an outdoor Mass, where Leo also addressed violence in society.
“Selfishness, injustice and evil are not overcome by brutality, but by prayer, patience and perseverance in denouncing what is wrong, by making our pleas with determination and working diligently to bring about the necessary changes,” said the leader of the Roman Catholic church.

items.title: Tchad : mobilisation contre le diabète à Mandalia

original_payload.original_title: Tchad : mobilisation contre le diabète à Mandalia
original_payload.original_body:
À l’occasion de la Journée mondiale du diabète, les Lions et Leos International Région 27 (Tchad) ont organisé, ce samedi 14 novembre, une activité de sensibilisation, de prévention et de dépistage à Mandalia, à environ 50 km au sud de N’Djamena.
L’objectif de cette activité est d’informer la population sur les causes, les symptômes et les moyens de prévention du diabète, tout en offrant un dépistage gratuit de la glycémie, notamment aux personnes à risque. Au programme : sensibilisation sur l’alimentation et l’activité physique, dépistages gratuits et conseils de santé individualisés.
Dans son mot de lancement, le président de la région 27, Tite Emmanuel Hounnoussa, a rappelé l’esprit de l’organisation : « Le diabète, quand il est découvert tôt, ne doit pas faire honte et ne doit pas pousser à abandonner. Son traitement est possible, à condition de respecter les conseils des médecins. Ce que vous apprenez ici, partagez-le avec votre famille et vos amis. Fidèle à notre devise, “Nous servons”».
Lire aussi :  « Le dépistage du diabète est indispensable pour prévenir ses complications », Dr Tchouagonbo Baïbamné
La maire adjointe de Mandalia, Haoua Mahamat Moumine, a salué le choix de sa ville : « Ce choix porté sur Mandalia permet à notre population de connaître sa situation, de savoir si elle a du diabète, de l’hypertension ou des problèmes de vue », a-t-elle confié.
Lançant officiellement la campagne, le gouverneur de l’organisation, Mahamat Malloum Oumar a alerté : « Le diabète tue, le diabète maltraite. Au Tchad, nous sommes à près de 600 000 cas. Si on ne prend pas garde, on sera à un million. On peut vivre avec cette maladie en respectant les conseils des médecins. La vue, c’est la vie, il faut tout faire pour éviter d’en arriver au pire. »
Lire aussi :  Santé : asthme, diabète de type 2, drépanocytose, ces maladies invisibles qui brisent des vies
Il a poursuivi en soulignant qu’il s’agit d’une maladie avec laquelle on peut vivre, à condition de respecter les consignes et les conseils donnés par les médecins et le personnel médical. C’est pourquoi, selon lui, la ville de Mandalia, historique et accueillante, avec une population laborieuse, a été choisie pour mener cette campagne afin que la maladie n’affecte ni les jeunes, ni les personnes âgées, ni les femmes, ni les hommes.
La population, venue en nombre après le marché, a bénéficié gratuitement des dépistages et des conseils, en présence des autorités locales du Chari-Baguirmi.

items.title: Tchad : Culturama organise un dépistage gratuit du diabète à N’Djamena

original_payload.original_title: Tchad : Culturama organise un dépistage gratuit du diabète à N’Djamena
original_payload.original_body:
À l’occasion de la Journée mondiale du diabète, célébrée le 14 novembre, l’association culturelle Culturama a organisé une journée de dépistage gratuit au stade Idriss Mahamat Ouya, à Assapa Village, dans le 3ᵉ arrondissement de N’Djamena. L’activité, menée en partenariat avec le ministère de la Santé publique et de la Prévention, avec l’appui de l’équipe médicale chinoise et de la Maison du diabète, était ouverte au public.
Cette initiative vise à sensibiliser les populations aux risques liés au diabète et à encourager le dépistage précoce. Elle a permis aux participants de connaître leur état de santé et, au besoin, d’être orientés vers des structures sanitaires pour une prise en charge adaptée.
Dans son mot d’ouverture, la présidente de Culturama, Claudine Alingué, a expliqué que le projet « Assapa Village » est né d’une histoire familiale. Le village porte le nom de sa mère, qui vivait avec le diabète et sensibilisait déjà son entourage à l’importance du dépistage et de la pratique du sport.
Lire aussi :  Prévention du diabète : les conseils du nutritionniste Yanwe Vincent Delsikreo
À travers cette initiative, l’association entend poursuivre cet engagement en faveur de la prévention. « Nous avons souhaité créer un espace accessible à tous, où les populations peuvent rencontrer des professionnels de santé, s’informer et bénéficier d’un dépistage gratuit », a-t-elle expliqué.
Prenant la parole à son tour, le président de la Maison du diabète, le Dr Djaury Dadjia, pédiatre-diabétologue, a insisté sur l’importance de la sensibilisation et du dépistage précoce.
Il a rappelé qu’un diagnostic réalisé à temps permet de limiter les risques de complications et d’orienter les personnes concernées vers des structures sanitaires pour une prise en charge médicale adaptée. Il a également invité les participants à profiter de cette campagne pour connaître leur état de santé.
Lire aussi :  Santé : asthme, diabète de type 2, drépanocytose, ces maladies invisibles qui brisent des vies
De son côté, le directeur général adjoint du ministère de la Jeunesse et des Sports, Youssouf Wadé, qui a procédé au lancement officiel de la cérémonie, a mis l’accent sur le rôle du sport dans la prévention des maladies.
Il a plaidé pour une pratique régulière de l’activité physique, particulièrement chez les jeunes, dans les établissements scolaires, les administrations et les quartiers. Selon lui, le sport doit être considéré comme un outil de prévention et un élément important de la promotion de la santé publique.
À travers cette première édition, Culturama ambitionne de faire d’Assapa Village un rendez-vous durable de sensibilisation, de prévention et de solidarité.
Cette journée de dépistage s’inscrit ainsi dans une démarche de prévention qui encourage les populations à ne pas attendre l’apparition des symptômes avant de consulter. « Agir tôt contre le diabète », tel est le message porté par les organisateurs.

items.title: 🕋 #حج2027 : هيئة تنظيم إدارة الحج والعمرة توقّع اتفاقية مع «فلاي أديل»، أحد أبرز الفاعلين في مجال نقل الحجاج جوًا

original_payload.original_title: 🕋 #حج2027 : هيئة تنظيم إدارة الحج والعمرة توقّع اتفاقية مع «فلاي أديل»، أحد أبرز الفاعلين في مجال نقل الحجاج جوًا
original_payload.original_body:
على هامش مؤتمر ومعرض الحج، المنعقد بمدينة جدة، وقّعت هيئة تنظيم إدارة الحج والعمرة (#أورجيب)، ممثلةً برئيسها الجنرال إدريس دوكوني الدكير، اتفاقية مع شركة الطيران السعودية «فلاي أديل» لنقل الحجاج التشاديين خلال موسم حج 1448هـ/2027م.
ووقّع الاتفاقية عن شركة «فلاي أديل» السيد إياد جمال الليل، مدير العمليات الأرضية والمدير بالإنابة لقطاع الحج والعمرة.
وتُعد «فلاي أديل»، التابعة لمجموعة الخطوط الجوية السعودية «السعودية»، من الشركات البارزة في مجال النقل الجوي داخل المملكة وعلى المستوى الدولي. وتشهد الشركة توسعًا متواصلًا، كما تمتلك أسطولًا حديثًا وخبرة خاصة في تنظيم العمليات الجوية المرتبطة بموسمي الحج والعمرة.
وخلال موسم حج 2026 وحده، نقلت الشركة أكثر من 145 ألف حاج قادمين من 13 دولة، ليرتفع بذلك إجمالي عدد حجاج بيت الله الحرام الذين نقلتهم منذ إطلاق عملياتها المخصصة للحج إلى أكثر من 600 ألف حاج.
وسبق لـ«فلاي أديل» أن كانت شريكًا لتشاد 🇹🇩 خلال موسمين سابقين من مواسم الحج، ما أكسبها معرفة جيدة بمتطلبات نقل الحجاج التشاديين.
ويتيح تجديد هذا التعاون البناء على الخبرة المشتركة المتراكمة، مع إيلاء اهتمام خاص بتخطيط الرحلات الجوية، والالتزام بالمواعيد، وانسيابية العمليات في المطارات، وحسن رعاية الحجاج، سواء عند المغادرة أو عند العودة.
وتُشكّل الخبرة التشغيلية التي تتمتع بها «فلاي أديل»، إلى جانب إمكاناتها الجوية وقدرتها على التنسيق، عوامل مهمة في دعم التحضيرات لموسم حج 2027.
وبالنسبة إلى هيئة تنظيم إدارة الحج والعمرة، تندرج هذه الاتفاقية في إطار نهج التحسين المستمر للخدمات المقدمة للحجاج التشاديين، استعدادًا لموسم يُرتقب أن يبلغ فيه عدد الحجاج التشاديين 7,000 حاج.
وتظل الغاية واحدة: الاستباق في مواجهة التحديات اللوجستية، وتحسين ظروف السفر، وتمكين الحجاج التشاديين من أداء فريضتهم في أفضل الظروف الممكنة.
#حج #أورجيب #تشا

items.title: Hadj 2027 : l’ORGEP signe un accord avec la compagnie aérienne saoudienne flyadeal

original_payload.original_title: Hadj 2027 : l’ORGEP signe un accord avec la compagnie aérienne saoudienne flyadeal
original_payload.original_body:
L’Organe de Régulation et de Gestion du Pèlerinage (ORGEP) a signé un accord avec la compagnie aérienne saoudienne flyadeal pour assurer le transport des pèlerins tchadiens lors du Hadj 2027, a annoncé l’organisme.
L’accord a été conclu à Djeddah, en marge du Salon et de la Conférence du Hadj, entre le président de l’ORGEP, le général Idriss Dokony Adiker, et Iyad Jamal Al-Lail, directeur des opérations au sol et directeur par intérim du Hadj et de la Omra de flyadeal.
Lire aussi :  Hadj 2027 : le président de l’ORGEP échange avec le ministre saoudien du Hadj et de la Omra
Filiale du groupe Saudia, flyadeal a transporté plus de 145 000 pèlerins de 13 pays lors du Hadj 2026, selon les chiffres communiqués par l’ORGEP. La compagnie avait déjà assuré le transport des pèlerins tchadiens lors de deux précédentes éditions.
Ce nouvel accord vise notamment à améliorer la planification des vols, la ponctualité et la prise en charge des pèlerins dans les aéroports, au départ comme au retour.
Lire aussi :  Hadj 2027 : le Tchad et l’Arabie saoudite scellent un accord pour l’organisation du pèlerinage
Le Tchad dispose d’un contingent de 7 000 pèlerins pour le Hadj 2027. L’ORGEP entend renforcer l’organisation logistique du pèlerinage afin d’améliorer les conditions de voyage des fidèles tchadiens.

items.title: Tchad : la télévision nationale lance son premier journal télévisé en langue des signes

original_payload.original_title: Tchad : la télévision nationale lance son premier journal télévisé en langue des signes
original_payload.original_body:
L’Office national des médias audiovisuels (ONAMA) a franchi une étape dans l’accès à l’information en diffusant, vendredi 13 novembre, pour la première fois au Tchad, un journal télévisé accompagné d’une interprétation en langue des signes, à destination des personnes sourdes et malentendantes.
Cette première édition a été assurée par Shalom, une interprète dont les deux parents sont sourds. «  Je trouve que c’est une responsabilité parce que j’ai mes deux parents qui sont sourds, papa tout comme maman  », a-t-elle confié avant sa prestation. À l’issue du journal, elle n’a pas caché son émotion : «  Je suis émue de joie. Je ne sais pas ce que je vais dire, mais en tout cas, ça s’est bien passé.  »
Pour le directeur de la Télévision nationale, Souleymane Djabo, cette initiative répond à une exigence d’inclusion. «  La langue des signes est une recommandation du Dialogue national souverain. Et le droit à l’information à tout Tchadien est une exigence de la télévision nationale  », a-t-il déclaré.
«  Nous avons franchi un cap important pour les sourds et les malentendants  », a-t-il ajouté, précisant que cette innovation, pour l’heure limitée au journal télévisé, sera progressivement étendue à d’autres programmes de la télévision nationale.
Cette initiative marque une avancée dans l’accessibilité de l’information audiovisuelle au Tchad, où les personnes sourdes et malentendantes disposent désormais d’un accès au journal télévisé national grâce à l’interprétation en langue des signes.
