items.title: Une vingtaine de journalistes reporters d’images des Agences de Presse Africaines en séminaire de formation à Rabat au Maroc

original_payload.original_title: Une vingtaine de journalistes reporters d’images des Agences de Presse Africaines en séminaire de formation à Rabat au Maroc
original_payload.original_body:
Par Tsahirou Abdoua, Envoyé Spécial de l’ANP
Rabat, 16 Novembre (ANP) – Le Président de la Fédération Atlantique des Agences de Presse Africaines (FAAPA), par ailleurs Directeur Général de l’Agence Maghreb Arabe de Presse (MAP, Maroc), M. Fouad Arif a présidé, ce lundi 16 novembre 2026 au Centre africain de formation des journalistes de la FAAPA, à Rabat au Maroc, la cérémonie d’ouverture d’un séminaire de formation des journalistes reporters d’images (JRI) des Agences des pays membres de ladite Organisation.
Autour du thème « Maîtrise des techniques du reportage vidéo : du tournage au montage », ce séminaire qui durera du 16 au 20 novembre regroupe une vingtaine de journalistes des agences de presse africaines.
Le Président de la FAAPA a informé que cette formation est inscrite dans le plan d’action de la FAAPA pour 2026, et que cette rencontre traduit une priorité commune : « renforcer les compétences de nos équipes pour accompagner la transformation de nos agences et développer une offre audiovisuelle de qualité ». M. Fouad Arif a saisi cette occasion pour adresser ses remerciements aux formateurs pour leur disponibilité et pour l’expertise qu’ils partageront durant ces cinq jours de formation. Il a également salué les équipes qui ont préparé cette formation, notamment le Secrétaire Général de la FAAPA.
Selon lui, « la vidéo occupe une place stratégique dans le développement de nos agences », précisant qu’elle « enrichit notre traitement de l’actualité, élargit nos audiences et nous permet de mieux répondre aux attentes des médias abonnés. Elle offre également des perspectives de diversification de nos services et de valorisation de nos contenus ».
Selon ses explications, cette évolution au niveau des agences de presse « doit s’appuyer sur ce qui fait notre force : notre présence sur le terrain, notre connaissance des réalités nationales et la crédibilité de notre information », soulignant que « ces atouts nous donnent une responsabilité particulière dans la manière dont l’Afrique est racontée et comprise ». Il a ainsi fait observer que « nous devons être en mesure de rendre compte, par l’image, des transformations de nos pays et des préoccupations de leurs citoyens ».
Dès lors, pour le DG de la MAP, « renforcer nos capacités audiovisuelles, c’est aussi affirmer la place des agences africaines dans la production et la circulation de l’information sur notre continent. Mais, a-t-il fait observer, cette ambition exige un investissement continu dans les compétences. D’où tout l’intérêt de cette formation qui doit permettre aux participants de mieux maîtriser les nouveaux outils et de mettre cette maîtrise au service de choix éditoriaux pertinents.
Le fait est qu’avec l’évolution technologique, « la qualité de nos productions repose sur la rigueur de notre travail », a-t-il poursuivi, affirmant que « le respect des faits et de la dignité des personnes, la vérification des sources et l’indépendance du jugement sont appelées à guider chaque décision de publication », faisant ainsi référence à l’intelligence artificielle qui renforce cette exigence, en ce que « son utilisation appelle un cadre éditorial clair et un contrôle humain effectif », même si « la responsabilité journalistique demeure la nôtre, quels que soient les outils employés ». Selon lui, en effet, « la confiance de nos publics dépend de notre capacité à tenir cette exigence ».
Par ailleurs, le Président Arif a rappelé que la FAAPA a vocation à faire de la coopération un appui concret au développement de ses membres, en s’appuyant sur le partage d’expertise et la mutualisation des expériences, qui « doivent nous permettre de progresser ensemble, en tenant compte des moyens et des besoins de chaque agence ».
Le responsable de la FAAPA a enfin souhaité que les acquis de ce séminaire se prolongent dans les rédactions, à travers la transmission des compétences aux collègues et le développement de la production vidéo. C’est dans cet esprit qu’il a invité à aborder ces cinq jours de formation avec le souci de transformer les connaissances partagées en progrès concrets pour les agences de presse, avant de souhaiter aux participants des travaux fructueux et un agréable séjour au Maroc.
TSA/KPM/ANP-120 Novembre 2026

items.title: POLICE NATIONALE : LE GÉNÉRAL ABOUBACAR OUMAROU, UN OFFICIER CHEVRONNÉ AUX COMMANDES

original_payload.original_title: POLICE NATIONALE : LE GÉNÉRAL ABOUBACAR OUMAROU, UN OFFICIER CHEVRONNÉ AUX COMMANDES
original_payload.original_body:
De la lutte contre le trafic illicite de stupéfiants aux responsabilités de commandement au sein de la Police nationale, le Commissaire général de police Aboubacar Issaka Oumarou prend les rênes de la DGPN. Son parcours est marqué par des expériences professionnelles au Niger et au sein de plusieurs missions internationales des Nations unies.
La Direction générale de la Police nationale (DGPN) connaît un nouveau changement à sa tête. Par décret signé le vendredi 13 novembre 2026, le président de la République, le général d’armée Abdourahamane Tiani, a nommé le Commissaire général de police Aboubacar Issaka Oumarou au poste de Directeur général de la Police nationale. Il succède à son prédécesseur après avoir dirigé l’Office central de répression du trafic illicite des stupéfiants (OCRTIS), une structure spécialisée dans la lutte contre les réseaux de trafic de drogues et de substances psychotropes.
Cette nomination place à la tête de la Police nationale un officier dont le parcours professionnel est marqué par une diversité d’expériences, aussi bien dans les services de sécurité intérieure que dans les opérations internationales de maintien de la paix.
Une formation policière au-delà des frontières
Le Commissaire général de police Aboubacar Issaka Oumarou dispose d’une formation acquise dans des établissements spécialisés de renom. Il est notamment diplômé de l’École nationale supérieure de police de Dakar, au Sénégal, ainsi que de l’École nationale supérieure de police de Saint-Cyr-au-Mont-d’Or, en France.
Ces formations constituent le socle d’un parcours professionnel au cours duquel il a occupé plusieurs postes de responsabilité au sein de la Police nationale nigérienne, aussi bien dans les services centraux que dans les structures déconcentrées.
Parmi ses fonctions antérieures figurent notamment celles de Directeur régional de la Police nationale à Agadez et de Directeur adjoint de la Sécurité publique. Avant sa nomination à la tête de la DGPN, il occupait le poste de Directeur général de l’OCRTIS.
À la tête de cet office spécialisé, il était chargé de contribuer à la conduite des opérations de lutte contre le trafic illicite de stupéfiants. Un domaine qui exige des compétences en matière d’investigation, de renseignement, de coordination opérationnelle et de coopération entre les différents services de sécurité .
Une expérience internationale au sein des Nations unies
L’un des aspects remarquables de son parcours réside également dans sa participation à plusieurs missions des Nations unies. Le Commissaire général Aboubacar Issaka Oumarou a notamment servi au Timor oriental, dans le cadre de l’UNTAET, au Burundi avec l’ONUB, ainsi qu’en République démocratique du Congo (RDC), au sein des missions MONUC et MONUSCO.
Au cours de ces missions, il a exercé différentes responsabilités, notamment celle de coordonnateur régional de la Police des Nations unies dans l’est de la RDC, avec résidence à Goma.
Il a également occupé les fonctions de directeur de projet chargé de la formation de six bataillons de la Police d’intervention rapide (PIR) de la Police nationale congolaise. Ce programme s’inscrivait dans le dispositif de sécurisation des élections générales de 2011 en RDC.
Son expérience internationale comprend aussi les fonctions de chef du groupe électoral de la Police des Nations unies. Ces différentes responsabilités l’ont amené à intervenir sur des questions liées à la sécurisation des processus électoraux, à la formation des unités spécialisées et à la coordination policière dans des environnements sécuritaires complexes.
Des défis sécuritaires importants
En prenant les commandes de la DGPN, le nouveau Directeur général hérite d’une institution confrontée à de nombreux défis. La lutte contre la criminalité organisée, le trafic de stupéfiants, la cybercriminalité, les réseaux de fraude et les différentes formes de délinquance figure parmi les principaux enjeux auxquels la Police nationale doit faire face.
À ces préoccupations s’ajoutent la nécessité de renforcer les capacités opérationnelles des unités, d’améliorer les conditions de travail des policiers et de consolider la collaboration entre les forces de sécurité et les populations.
Son passage à l’OCRTIS et ses expériences au sein des missions onusiennes constituent des atouts dans son parcours professionnel. Reste désormais à savoir comment cette expérience sera mise à profit dans la conduite de la Police nationale et dans la réponse aux attentes sécuritaires des Nigériens.
Au-delà du changement de responsable, cette nomination ouvre une nouvelle séquence pour la DGPN. Les résultats du nouveau Directeur général seront notamment appréciés à l’aune de l’efficacité opérationnelle de l’institution, de sa proximité avec les citoyens et de sa capacité à assurer la protection des personnes et des biens dans le respect des lois de la République.
Abdoulaziz Moussa

items.title: Guinea's gold rush: Arrests, deportations spark outcry

original_payload.original_title: Guinea's gold rush: Arrests, deportations spark outcry
original_payload.original_body:
Politics   Guinea
Guinea's gold rush: Arrests, deportations spark outcry
Nikolas Fischer
11/16/2026  November 16, 2026    Guinea has banned illegal gold mining, citing environmental concerns. It has further charged hundreds of suspected local and foreign illegal miners amid reports of rights abuses and deportations.
https://p.dw.com/p/5PLa6
Prefer DW on Google
Guinea wants to start refining some of its gold locally Image: A_STOCK1992/Depositphotos/IMAGO       Advertisement
In Siguiri, northeastern  Guinea , the  gold  rush has come to an abrupt end. "To date, 1,263 people, including Guineans, Burkinabe, Malians, Togolese, Nigerians, Ivorians, and Ghanaians, have been arrested and taken to Conakry for legal proceedings," Guinea's army spokesman, General Mamadou Aliou Sow, said. He added that officers from the Criminal Investigation Division, the National Police, and the National Gendarmerie are currently conducting interrogations.
The operation follows the ban on  illegal gold mining  in the Siguiri administrative region. According to Guinean authorities, the aim is to stop mining practices considered harmful to the environment.  Uncontrolled gold mining depletes the soil , destroys vegetation and chokes waterways.
For many West Africans, including Guinea, artisanal mining is a key source of livelihood  Image: Mike Goldwater/Visually/picture alliance
"We know that there have recently been various forms of gold mining here involving the use of chemicals that can  destroy the environment and pollute our water sources," Toumany Sangare, chairman of the Siguiri civil society council, told DW.
The closure of the mining sites is having a significant impact on the local economy. For many workers, it means the sudden loss of their main source of income. DW spoke with young gold panners from  Burkina Faso  who had been driven out of Siguiri. Some said they had walked more than 200 km (124 miles) to the Malian capital, Bamako.
"We tried our luck, but just as we were beginning to feel hopeful, we were told to leave," Noufa, in his early 20s,  who arrived in Siguiri in early October to work in a small mine, told DW. Another Burkinabe, who goes by the name Mc One, told DW he set out for Siguiri to earn money to provide for his elderly parents and relatives. "I left just under five months ago. We went through very difficult times there."
Did Guinean authorities target foreigners?
Guinean authorities  refute the allegation that the ban on gold mining specifically targeted foreigners, saying the measure applies to all illegal gold miners. The closure of the mine primarily affects Guineans, Mohamed Nabe, chairman of the Committee on Mining and Industry, told DW.
"Millions of  Guineans  are affected by this, compared to just a few thousand foreigners," Nabe said, adding that like everywhere else, there are cross-border population movements. "Of course, this can raise certain security concerns, but it was not the security aspect that motivated this decision. The main reasons are environmental in nature, as well as the need to better organize, structure, and regulate the mining sector."
The hidden cost of illegal gold mining in Ghana
To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that  supports HTML5 video
Supporting the move, Morissanda Kouyate, Guinea's Foreign Minister, said his country is not the only one to ban illegal gold mining. However, according to Burkina Faso's Minister of Security, Mahamadou Sana, the deported nationals were allegedly subjected to "cruel, inhuman, and degrading treatment." He spoke of "brutality" and alleged that the operation had resulted in deaths and injuries.
Malian journalist Amadou Oumar Diallo also criticized the alleged brutality of the Guinean authorities. In his view, they violated human rights. "Normally, when you prevent someone from exercising their freedom, you also have to provide for them," Diallo told DW. "This care is expensive. Detention alone costs a lot of money.  The Guinean government  took the easy way out by refusing to adhere to these principles and deporting all these people."
While Burkina Faso strongly condemned the treatment of gold panners, Mali's leadership initially adopted a somewhat more restrained tone. Officially, Bamako described Guinea's decision to expel the miners as "sovereign."
Most recently, however, Mali's Prime Minister, Major General Abdoulaye Maiga, spoke of a "humanitarian catastrophe." On November 8, he traveled to Kouremale on the border between  Mali  and Guinea, where dozens of deported Malians were returning to the country. Given the close ties between Mali and Guinea, Maiga regretted the lack of coordination between the two countries.
Currently, authorities in Mali and Burkina Faso are organizing efforts to assist their citizens: buses and trucks have been mobilized from both Bamako and Ouagadougou to bring the deported gold miners back to their home countries.
Guinea opens its first gold refinery
Parallel to the events in Siguiri, the  Nimba Gold Refinery (NGR)     has begun operations in Conakry. With this, Guinea joins other West African nations such as Burkina Faso, Mali, and  Cote d'Ivoire . The Guinean government's goal is to refine 30% of the 70 metric tons (70,000 kg) of gold mined in the country domestically.
Dr. Ibrahim Diallo, a mining expert, suggested that the Guinean authorities may have wanted to bring the gold mines in Siguiri under their control to supply the Nimba Gold Refinery (NGR). "What's happening in Siguiri isn't gold panning. A gold panner doesn't use a bulldozer or an excavator."
Joining forces to protect Guinea's Tristao Islands
To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that  supports HTML5 video
Patrick Schein, chairman of the Alliance for Responsible Mining (ARM), told DW that it made more sense for Guinea to build up reserves with domestic gold rather than imported gold. However, he also stressed that the gold must be certified to be internationally recognized.
He does not anticipate significant local demand, so  exports are crucial . It remains to be seen whether the refinery in Conakry can be competitive in this regard. For jewelry manufacturing, for example, international-level technical expertise is required.
Another issue, according to the ARM chairman, is that the location of refining determines the gold's origin. "So if I'm in Guinea and import or buy gold that comes from another country, that gold becomes Guinean gold through local refining," Schein said. "If Guinea serves as a transit hub for gold from the subregion, it would—unintentionally—become a center for money laundering," he added.
According to Schein, tracing refined gold is harder than tracing raw gold. However, if the goal of refining [gold] in Guinea is to ensure better traceability,  pay miners better wages  and create a mercury-free processing chain, then that is a good initiative. "But now this must also be put into practice."
Mohamed Toure in Conakry and Mahamadou Kane in Bamako contributed to this article
This article was originally written in German

items.title: Germany, EU states open talks on Rwanda deportation scheme

original_payload.original_title: Germany, EU states open talks on Rwanda deportation scheme
original_payload.original_body:
Migration    Germany
Germany joins 4 other EU states in Rwanda deportation hub talks
Alex Berry   with Reuters, AFP
11/16/2026  November 16, 2026    The move follows approval of EU regulations that ease deportations and allow hubs to be set up outside the bloc. A similar scheme by the UK government fell apart over legal issues.
https://p.dw.com/p/5PV1q
Prefer DW on Google
The European Union has struggled to find a migration policy that satisfies all member states Image: Daniel Kubirski/IMAGO       Advertisement
A group of five EU member states, including Germany, will begin talks on a new scheme to deport rejected  asylum seekers  to Rwanda, the Austrian government said on Monday.
A plan to set up so-called return hubs in a non-EU country had been announced by the group — which also includes Austria, the Netherlands, Greece and Denmark —   back in September .
Monday's announcement comes after the  EU introduced new regulations  to speed up deportations and allow the establishment of hubs outside of the bloc.
What do we know about the EU deportation hub scheme?
Rwanda  had not been officially named as the chosen country , but people who had been briefed on the ongoing negotiations spoke to Reuters and AFP news agencies.
The central African country had also acknowledged being in "preliminary discussions" with the group of states.
Rwanda had also been the intended destination for a similar plan set up under the UK's former Conservative government that  subsequently collapsed in UK courts .
'Migration paradox': How borders, aid drive human movement
To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that  supports HTML5 video
However, the new EU scheme differs from the British one in that it is only intended for migrants who have exhausted all other legal avenues within the European Union.
Migration hubs have been seen by governments as a means to visibly show that they are taking action on migration amid surging anti-migrant sentiment and rising support for the far right.
What are the criticisms of the deportation hub plans?
While the leaders of the five countries said the scheme would comply with EU law, that has not protected them from criticism, especially over the plan to send migrants to a country with which they have no connection.
The Council of Europe, a pan-European human rights body, said in July that return hubs posed "considerable human rights risks."
Claims that the scheme is meant as a deterrence have been rejected by researchers who say there is no evidence that deterrence works.
"Enforcement changes how people travel, not whether they travel. Some pause or ⁠change ​route, and smugglers adapt and raise their prices," said Roberto Forin of the Mixed Migration Centre, a ​research institute that collects data along migration routes.
The choice to pick Rwanda has also been controversial, with the government of President Paul Kagame in particular being accused of suppressing dissent and supporting the M23 rebel group in the neighboring Democratic Republic of Congo.
"Paying Kigali [Rwanda] to host a deportation program would not only cause suffering and harm to those deported, it would finance and provide political leverage to a government responsible for serious human rights abuses at home and abroad," said Human Rights Watch's senior Africa researcher, Clementine de Montjoye.
Rwanda unscathed in failed UK migration deal

items.title: NASARAWA DEPUTY GOVERNOR DECLARES 67TH NATIONAL COUNCIL ON HEALTH TECHNICAL SESSION OPEN

original_payload.original_title: NASARAWA DEPUTY GOVERNOR DECLARES 67TH NATIONAL COUNCIL ON HEALTH TECHNICAL SESSION OPEN
original_payload.original_body:
-Gaza Charges Delegates to Enjoy the Hospitality of Lafia
The Deputy Governor of Nasarawa State, Dr. Emmanuel Akabe, has formally declared open the Technical Session of the 67th National Council on Health (NCH), expressing the state government’s appreciation to the Federal Ministry of Health and Social Welfare for choosing Lafia, the state capital, to host the national meeting.
Dr. Akabe, who represented the Governor of Nasarawa State, Engr. Abdullahi Sule, at the opening ceremony, described the hosting of the Council as a privilege and an opportunity to showcase the state’s hospitality, peaceful environment and economic potential.
The Deputy Governor, a former Commissioner for Health in Nasarawa State (2011–2015), noted that he was familiar with the Council’s proceedings, having last attended a meeting in 2014, also expressed confidence that the deliberations, guided by the theme, “From Commitment to Results: Delivering Quality and Equitable Healthcare for All Nigerians,” would produce practical resolutions capable of strengthening healthcare delivery across the country.
He further emphasised the importance of translating the commitments and discussions of the Council into measurable outcomes, expressing optimism that the technical deliberations and subsequent communiqué would provide actionable recommendations for improving Nigeria’s health sector.
Dr. Akabe reaffirmed Nasarawa State’s commitment to supporting national health sector reforms and ensuring a successful meeting, urging delegates and participants, to enjoy the hospitality and peaceful atmosphere of the state.
On behalf of the Governor and the people of Nasarawa State, the Deputy Governor formally declared the Technical Session of the 67th National Council on Health open, wishing participants fruitful deliberations and successful outcomes.
Earlier in his welcome remarks, the Nasarawa State Commissioner for Health, Dr. Gwamna Gaza, has welcomed delegates and participants to the Technical Session of the 67th National Council on Health (NCH), expressing the State Government’s commitment to ensuring a successful and fruitful Council meeting in Lafia, Nasarawa State.
Dr. Gaza, recalled that Nasarawa State was unanimously endorsed to host the 67th NCH at the previous Council meeting held in Calabar, Cross River State, about 12 months ago.
He expressed appreciation to the Honourable Commissioners of Health and other stakeholders for supporting the State’s hosting bid, describing the occasion as a historic opportunity for Nasarawa State to welcome health sector leaders from across the country for the first time.
While welcoming the Coordinating Minister of Health and Social Welfare and other council members in advance; the Commissioner welcomed the Permanent Secretary of the Federal Ministry of Health and Social Welfare, State Permanent Secretaries, heads of health agencies, directors, development partners and members of the media, and assured participants of the State’s hospitality and a conducive environment for constructive deliberations.
He noted that the decisions reached at the Council would have significant implications for the Nigerian health sector, stressing that health sector leaders must remain conscious that they are also beneficiaries of the policies and reforms they formulate on behalf of Nigerians.
The Commissioner further encouraged participants to engage actively and communicate any challenges encountered during their stay, assuring them that the State’s health leadership and relevant institutions were available to provide necessary assistance.
He highlighted Nasarawa State’s identity as a home of solid minerals, hospitality and welcoming people, while expressing optimism that participants would enjoy their stay and contribute meaningfully to the deliberations.
Dr. Gaza wished all delegates a successful and productive Council meeting and formally welcomed them to Lafia, Nasarawa State.
Presenting the procedures of the Technical Session, the Permanent Secretary of the Ministry and Chairman of the Technical Committee of the meeting, Daju Kachollom S. mni, the two-day Technical Committee meeting scheduled for 16–17 November 2026, would provide the technical foundation for the Council meeting scheduled for 19–20 November 2026, to be chaired by the Coordinating Minister of Health and Social Welfare.
She stated that the Technical Committee would review the proceedings and implementation status of resolutions of the 66th Regular National Council on Health, consider memoranda submitted by the Federal Ministry, States and other Ministries, and develop recommendations for consideration by the Council.
The Permanent Secretary, who announced that the 67th NCH would be her last meeting, further disclosed that memoranda for the meeting had been organised around the four pillars of the Health Sector Strategic Blueprint: Effective Governance; Efficient, Equitable and Quality Health System; Unlocking Value Chains; and Health Security.
She added that the thematic areas cover strengthening implementation of the National Health Act, promoting multisectoral health interventions, advancing clinical research and development, and improving the country’s capacity to detect, prevent and respond to public health threats, including cholera, Lassa fever, cerebrospinal meningitis and measles.
To ensure focused and productive discussions, she explained that summaries of the memoranda had been prepared as working documents, while authors would be given five minutes each to present the title and purpose of their submissions, summarise key issues and state their recommendations. “The Secretariat will subsequently consolidate the Technical Committee’s recommendations for consideration by the Council.” The Permanent Secretary further stated.
Emphasising the Ministry’s commitment to efficient and technology-driven coordination, the Permanent Secretary noted that the National Council on Health continues to operate an electronic documentation system, with all relevant meeting documents preloaded onto tablets provided to participants, encouraging members to utilise the digital platform, assuring them of technical support from the NCH Secretariat and ICT team.
She urged participants to make meaningful technical contributions, maintain brevity in their interventions and focus on practical recommendations that would strengthen health sector performance and accelerate the delivery of quality, equitable and accessible healthcare to Nigerians.
The meeting will also feature presentations and interactive sessions on the 67th NCH theme, “From Commitments to Results: Delivering Quality and Equitable Health Care for All Nigerians,” and its sub-themes, including tracking the implementation of National Council on Health resolutions, improving quality service delivery at the Primary Health Care level, data-driven decision-making and digital health, and promoting equitable access to quality health services across States and vulnerable populations.
Ado Bako
Assistant Director, Information and Public Relations.

original_payload.original_title: FAAPA president urges African agencies to strengthen video production
original_payload.original_body:
General News  FAAPA president urges African agencies to strengthen video production
By  Fatimah Muhammed   ·   1 hour ago   ·  2 min read
✓
✓
FAAPA president urges African agencies to strengthen video production
By Daniel Obaje
Rabat, Nov. 16, 2026 (NAN) President of the Federation of African Press Agencies (FAAPA), Fouad Arif, has urged African news agencies to strengthen their audio-visual capacities to improve news coverage, expand audiences and diversify their services.
Arif, who is also the Director-General of Maghreb Arabe Presse (MAP), made the call on Monday in Rabat, Morocco, at the opening of a five-day seminar for journalists and image reporters from FAAPA member agencies.
He said “video plays a strategic role in the development of news agencies, enriching news coverage and  creating opportunities to expand services.
“It also broadens audiences and allows better response to the expectations of subscribed media, as well as offer opportunities for diversifying services and enhancing content.”
Arif said African agencies must also build on their strengths, knowledge of national realities and credibility of information to ensure that the continent is accurately represented.
He added that “our progress must build on our strengths, our understanding of national realities and the credibility of our information.
“The strength gives us special responsibility to ensure that Africa is accurately represented and understood.
“We must tell the stories of our countries’ development and reflect the concerns of the citizens.”
The FAAPA boss explained that strengthening audio-visual capacities would also affirm the position of African agencies in the production and circulation of information across the continent.
Arif stressed that “achieving this ambition requires continuous investment in professional development and mastery of new tools.”
He emphasised the need for professionalism and ethical standards in media production, particularly respect for facts, human dignity, verification of sources and editorial independence.
He said public confidence in the media depends on the ability of journalists and news agencies to uphold these standards.
He reiterated FAAPA’s commitment to supporting the development of its member agencies through the sharing of expertise and exchange of experiences, taking into account their different resources and needs.
He urged participants to share the knowledge acquired with colleagues in their respective newsrooms and promote video production.
The five-day seminar, holding from Nov. 16 to Nov. 20, focuses on mastering video reporting techniques from shooting to editing. (NAN)
DANO/HA

✓
✓
By Funmilayo Adeyemi
The Nigerian Library Association (NLA) has appealed to Gov. Uba Sani of Kaduna State to halt plans to relocate the Kaduna State Library Board headquarters to Zaria.
The ​‌⁠⁠‌‌‍⁠⁠‍‍‍​​‍‌‍⁠‌​association’s President, Dr Lawal Umar, made the appeal at a news conference in Abuja on Monday.
Umar said the proposed relocation, intended to accommodate the state judiciary, could undermine public library services and restrict citizens’ access to essential information resources.
“We recognise the importance of the judiciary and the need to provide appropriate accommodation for its operations.
“We strongly believe that such an arrangement should not be pursued at the expense of public library services and the accessibility of these essential institutions to the citizens,” he said.
He acknowledged the need to provide suitable accommodation for the judiciary but urged the state government to consider alternative government buildings within Kaduna city.
“We therefore appeal to His Excellency to direct an immediate halt to the relocation, adequately fund and strengthen the Kaduna State Library Board.
“The governor should consider providing the judiciary with another suitable government building within Kaduna city,” he said.
Umar said the government could address the legitimate accommodation needs of the judiciary without compromising the mandate, identity, relevance and accessibility of the state’s public library system.
He said the appeal was aimed at protecting public institutions, preserving access to information and ensuring that library services remained a priority in the state’s development agenda.
Umar expressed confidence that the governor and other relevant stakeholders would give the association’s appeal favourable consideration.(NAN)

items.title: Make libraries mental wellness hubs, NLA urges governments

original_payload.original_title: Make libraries mental wellness hubs, NLA urges governments
original_payload.original_body:
Education  Make libraries mental wellness hubs, NLA urges governments
By  Funmilayo Adeyemi   ·   1 hour ago   ·  3 min read
✓
✓
By Funmilayo Adeyemi
The Nigerian Library Association (NLA) has urged governments at all levels to integrate libraries into mental health promotion and public enlightenment programmes.
The association said the move would help address growing mental health challenges in the country.
NLA President, Dr Lawal Umar, made the call at a news conference to mark the 2026 Library Week in Abuja on Monday.
Umar said libraries could promote mental health awareness by providing credible information, safe spaces and access to relevant support services.
“What has librarianship got to do with mental health? The answer is that libraries are much more than repositories of books and information resources.
“Today, modern libraries across the globe are evolving into community wellness hubs and safe sanctuaries.
“Libraries intersect with mental health,” he said.
He said the theme of the 2026 Library Week, “Libraries and Mental Health”, was chosen to highlight growing mental health challenges across homes, schools, workplaces and communities.
According to him, up to 30 per cent of Nigerians may experience a mental health condition during their lifetime, while the treatment gap exceeds 80 per cent.
He added that other studies estimated that about 20 per cent of Nigerians experienced mental health conditions, with limited access to adequate care.
Umar identified poverty, unemployment, insecurity, substance abuse, academic pressure and stigma as factors worsening the situation.
He said libraries were evolving beyond repositories of books and information resources into community spaces capable of supporting mental well-being.
“Libraries promote mental health awareness and literacy by providing access to credible information on mental health conditions, prevention, treatment and available support services.
“Libraries curate and disseminate accurate, culturally relevant and evidence-based mental health resources.
“They empower citizens to recognise early warning signs, understand that mental illness is treatable, and connect with verified medical and psychological support,” he said.
He explained that libraries could also provide welcoming and inclusive spaces where people could read, reflect, interact and temporarily escape everyday pressures.
The NLA president said reading, storytelling, creative writing and group discussions could reduce stress and isolation while building emotional resilience.
He, however, stressed that librarians were not expected to diagnose or treat mental health conditions.
Rather, he said, their responsibility was to promote awareness, provide credible information and facilitate referrals to qualified professionals.
Umar said activities scheduled for Nov. 16 to Nov. 20 included public lectures, seminars, mental health awareness campaigns, road walks, library exhibitions and community outreach programmes.
Others included debates, essay competitions, media campaigns and workshops to equip librarians with basic mental health literacy and referral knowledge.
He urged state chapters, professional sections, academic, public and school libraries to organise activities addressing the mental health needs of their respective communities.
Umar also called for stronger collaboration among libraries, healthcare institutions, educational establishments, civil society organisations and development partners.
He urged federal, state and local governments to strengthen funding for public, school and academic libraries.
He also advocated support for the provision of credible health information resources in libraries.
The NLA president called for closer collaboration between the Ministries of Health and Education to integrate libraries into implementing the National Mental Health Act.(NAN)

items.title: Corporate lessons from Dangote’s social responsibility model

original_payload.original_title: Corporate lessons from Dangote’s social responsibility model
original_payload.original_body:
General News  Corporate lessons from Dangote’s social responsibility model
By  Abdulrahman Kadiri   ·   2 hours ago   ·  8 min read
✓
✓
By Ismail Abdulaziz,  News Agency of Nigeria (NAN)
With 133 million Nigerians living in multidimensional poverty, corporate investment in education, healthcare, water supply and economic empowerment remains an important complement to government development efforts.
The 2022 National Multidimensional Poverty Index (MPI) survey by the National Bureau of Statistics (NBS) found that 63 per cent of Nigeria’s population experienced multiple deprivations.
These included inadequate sanitation, limited access to healthcare, food insecurity and poor housing.
Similarly, the 2024 Nigeria Demographic and Health Survey (NDHS) found that only 38 per cent of households had drinking water on their premises, while 20 per cent of the household population practised open defaecation.
These figures underscore the development challenges confronting many communities and the need for sustained investment by government, development partners and the private sector.
Against this backdrop, Corporate Social Responsibility (CSR) has become an important instrument through which businesses can contribute to social development while building sustainable relationships with their host communities.
Among Nigeria’s prominent philanthropic initiatives is the Aliko Dangote Foundation (ADF), established by Africa’s industrialist, Aliko Dangote, to support health, education, economic empowerment and humanitarian interventions.
In March 2014, Dangote made an endowment of 1.25 billion dollars to the foundation to strengthen its capacity to expand its interventions in health, education and economic empowerment.
The foundation’s approach reflects a broader understanding of philanthropy, moving beyond occasional charitable donations towards structured investments in human development and poverty reduction.
However, beyond the foundation’s philanthropic activities, Dangote Group’s CSR programmes across its industrial locations provide another perspective on how businesses can contribute to community development.
For many rural communities hosting large industrial establishments, the arrival of a major company raises expectations that extend beyond employment opportunities and commercial activities.
Residents often look forward to improved infrastructure, access to social amenities, educational opportunities, healthcare services and greater participation in the local economy.
Across several of its host communities, Dangote’s CSR interventions have attracted commendations from traditional rulers, community leaders and beneficiaries, who say the initiatives have helped address some longstanding developmental challenges.
From scholarships and healthcare outreaches to boreholes, roads and skills-acquisition programmes, the interventions have provided support to residents in different locations.
In Ibeju-Lekki, Lagos, where the Dangote Petroleum Refinery is located, community stakeholders have reportedly welcomed interventions such as access-road rehabilitation, water provision, scholarships and technical training.
For residents, these initiatives are important in a rapidly developing industrial environment where population growth and increased economic activities can place additional pressure on existing infrastructure and social services.
Community leaders, including the traditional ruler of Magbon-Segun, Mufutau Dauda, have acknowledged the benefits of the company’s interventions.
Similarly, Shakiru Bello, the traditional ruler of Okeyanta, commended the scholarship programme, noting its relevance in supporting families and students.
Such interventions, especially in education, can reduce the financial burden on parents while expanding opportunities for children from disadvantaged backgrounds.
Beyond Lagos, communities hosting Dangote Cement’s operations in other parts of the country have also benefited from similar interventions.
In Obajana, Kogi, where Dangote Cement operates one of its major plants, community stakeholders have acknowledged the company’s contributions to educational development, healthcare, infrastructure and employment.
Scholarships, schools, healthcare facilities, concrete roads and skills-acquisition programmes have featured among the reported interventions.
For many residents of industrial host communities, access to these facilities represents practical improvements in their quality of life.
In Gboko, Benue, community feedback has similarly highlighted the importance of water provision, electricity and educational support.
Chief Zaki Anum, district head of Mbatyu, expressed satisfaction with the provision of a borehole in his community, describing the intervention as beneficial to residents.
The importance of such an intervention becomes clearer against the background of Nigeria’s water access challenges.
According to the 2024 NDHS, although 71 per cent of the household population had at least basic drinking water services, only 38 per cent of households had water on their premises.
A borehole, therefore, is more than an infrastructure project.
Where properly maintained and supported by effective water management, it can reduce the time spent fetching water, improve hygiene and contribute to better public health.
Similarly, in Okpella, Edo, beneficiaries of a free malaria treatment programme organised by Dangote Cement in May 2024 expressed appreciation for the intervention.
Mrs Adiza Aliu said the programme enabled her to receive treatment without payment, while Innocent Valetina described it as a relief for families struggling with the cost of medicines.
These experiences illustrate how community-based healthcare interventions can provide immediate support to households, especially those with limited access to affordable medical services.
The scale of such corporate interventions is also reflected in Dangote Cement’s 2024 Sustainability Report.
The company reported that it spent N12.421 billion on social investment projects in 2024, representing a 427 per cent increase from N2.356 billion recorded in 2023.
It also reported completing 71 community projects and engaging 773 community stakeholders during the year.
Furthermore, the company partnered with the New Nigeria Foundation in January 2024 to conduct a needs assessment across 17 host communities around its Ibese plant in Ogun.
The assessment identified healthcare, education, infrastructure and economic empowerment as priority areas for community development.
These figures provide an indication of the resources committed to social investment and the importance of identifying community needs before implementing development projects.
Nevertheless, the effectiveness of CSR programmes cannot be measured solely by the amount of money spent or the number of projects executed.
Rather, their impact depends on whether the interventions respond to residents’ priorities, reach intended beneficiaries and remain functional over time.
In spite of the reported achievements, community satisfaction with CSR programmes is not always uniform, as residents have different expectations from companies operating in their areas.
For communities hosting large industrial establishments, the presence of a company often creates expectations that qualified indigenes will enjoy greater access to employment and business opportunities.
Although companies may employ thousands of workers, perceptions of fairness in recruitment, especially for skilled and managerial positions, can significantly influence community relations.
Environmental concerns also remain central to the relationship between companies and their host communities.
Around cement manufacturing and mining operations, issues such as dust emissions, noise, land degradation, water pollution and pressure on local infrastructure can influence residents’ perceptions of corporate responsibility.
Dangote Cement’s 2024 Sustainability Report acknowledges the need to assess potential effects on soil, air quality, noise levels and water pollution before implementing projects.
The report also indicates that the company conducted stakeholder assessments involving 2,222 participants, including employees, customers, investors, suppliers and host communities.
This highlights the importance of incorporating environmental and social concerns into corporate development strategies rather than treating CSR as a separate charitable activity.
Consequently, while social investment is important, effective corporate responsibility must also involve responsible environmental management, transparent communication and continuous engagement with affected residents.
The challenge, therefore, is to ensure that CSR interventions are not only visible but also responsive to the broader and evolving needs of host communities.
From a development perspective, corporate social responsibility should go beyond philanthropic assistance to establish mutually beneficial relationships between businesses and the communities in which they operate.
For companies such as Dangote Group, whose operations involve substantial investments and extensive industrial activities, structured community engagement is particularly important.
The application of Community Development Agreements (CDAs) provides a framework for defining responsibilities, establishing priorities and improving accountability between companies and host communities.
When properly implemented, such agreements can help reduce misunderstandings, improve trust and ensure that interventions are aligned with the developmental needs of residents.
However, their effectiveness depends on the extent to which commitments are fulfilled, beneficiaries are fairly selected and completed projects are properly maintained.
The experiences of host communities across Dangote Group’s operational locations demonstrate how CSR can serve as an instrument for improving social welfare and strengthening corporate-community relations.
The reported investments in scholarships, healthcare programmes, water provision and infrastructure suggest that private-sector interventions can complement government efforts to address development challenges.
At the same time, concerns surrounding employment, environmental impact, project adequacy and sustainability highlight areas requiring continuous attention.
As Nigeria continues to pursue industrialisation and economic diversification, the relationship between major corporations and their host communities will remain an important component of sustainable development.
Dangote’s CSR programmes, therefore, offer an opportunity to examine how private-sector investments can contribute to addressing infrastructure and social development challenges while promoting peaceful coexistence.
Ultimately, the success of any corporate social responsibility model should be measured not only by the resources committed but also by the lasting improvements it brings to people’s lives.
Residents of communities hosting Dangote’s operations expect the gains recorded to be sustained and outstanding concerns addressed.
They also want stronger industry-community partnerships to promote inclusive and sustainable development. (NANFeatures)

items.title: Nigeria records 185 open defecation-free LGAs – FG

original_payload.original_title: Nigeria records 185 open defecation-free LGAs – FG
original_payload.original_body:
Environment  Nigeria records 185 open defecation-free LGAs – FG
By  Tosin Kolade   ·   3 hours ago   ·  3 min read
✓
✓
By Eniola Elewude
The Federal Government says 185 Local Government Areas (LGAs) have attained Open Defecation Free (ODF) status, while Jigawa and Katsina have achieved state-wide ODF status.
The Minister of Water Resources and Sanitation, Prof. Joseph Utsev, disclosed this on Monday in Abuja at a news conference ahead of the 2026 World Toilet Day and seventh anniversary of the Clean Nigeria Campaign.
Utsev said the achievements resulted from collaboration among the three tiers of government, development partners, civil society organisations, the private sector and communities.
He, however, said intensified efforts were needed to achieve Nigeria’s target of ending open defecation by 2030 and sustain existing ODF achievements.
The minister said President Bola Tinubu had signed the Executive Order on Open Defecation Free Nigeria by 2030 and Other Related Matters, 2025, to strengthen coordination, clarify responsibilities and promote accountability among government institutions.
He said Vice-President Kashim Shettima would formally unveil the order during the World Toilet Day celebration on Nov. 19.
Utsev urged relevant Ministries, Departments and Agencies, state governments and local government authorities to implement their respective responsibilities under the order.
He identified sustainable financing, reliable data and monitoring, and institutional strengthening as priorities for accelerating progress towards the 2030 target.
He called on governments at all levels to make adequate budgetary provisions for sanitation, improve resource utilisation and encourage private sector investment.
The minister also urged states to strengthen sanitation reporting systems and regularly monitor performance to identify gaps and guide interventions.
He stressed the need to integrate the campaign into state and local government programmes, promote consistent toilet use and maintain sanitation facilities to prevent communities from reverting to open defecation.
Utsev said the ministry had scheduled a two-day annual retreat for states on the campaign from Nov. 17 to Nov. 18.
The retreat is themed, “Accelerating and Sustaining Progress: Financing, Data, and Systems for a Fully ODF Nigeria”.
It will bring together government representatives, development partners and other stakeholders to review progress and develop strategies for achieving nationwide ODF status.
He said the World Toilet Day celebration on Nov. 19 would be held alongside the campaign’s seventh anniversary, with the theme, “Sanitation and Gender Equality”.
According to him, the event would promote inclusive sanitation and recognise LGAs that had attained ODF status.
The minister urged state governors, local government chairmen, traditional and religious leaders, development partners and community leaders to strengthen their support for the campaign.
He also called on Nigerians to make toilet use a daily practice, stressing that ending open defecation required collective action.
Earlier, the Director Overseeing the Office of the Permanent Secretary in the ministry, Ali Dallah, said achieving an ODF Nigeria by 2030 required sustained political commitment, increased investment in sanitation infrastructure and stronger institutional coordination.
Dallah also stressed the need for reliable monitoring systems, continuous behavioural change interventions and measures to prevent communities from losing their ODF status.
He described the media as a critical partner in the campaign, urging journalists to sustain public awareness and mobilise communities towards ending open defecation.
The Clean Nigeria: Use the Toilet Campaign was launched in November 2019 to promote safe sanitation and end open defecation in Nigeria.
The campaign supports Sustainable Development Goal 6.2, which targets universal access to adequate sanitation and hygiene by 2030. (  NAN  )

original_payload.original_title: 2027: Showunmi ​‌‌​‍‍‍‍⁠⁠‍‍‌⁠⁠​‌​‍‌​urges NSA to enforce political discipline for national security
original_payload.original_body:
General News  2027: Showunmi ​‌‌​‍‍‍‍⁠⁠‍‍‌⁠⁠​‌​‍‌​urges NSA to enforce political discipline for national security
By  Olawunmi Ashafa   ·   3 hours ago   ·  3 min read
✓
✓
By Abiodun Lawal
Mr Segun Showunmi, a former aide to Atiku Abubakar, has urged the National Security Adviser (NSA), Malam Nuhu Ribadu, to enforce political discipline and accountability in the interest of national security.
Showunmi made the appeal in an open letter to Ribadu, a copy of which was made available to newsmen in Abeokuta on Monday.
He expressed concern over what he described as the growing toxicity of political conduct, reckless political communication and inflammatory statements by politicians and their supporters.
According to him, political competition, personal ambition and partisan disagreements should not be allowed to become additional threats to national stability.
Showunmi stressed the need to distinguish between legitimate political engagement and conduct capable of inciting violence, promoting ethnic or religious hostility, and undermining national cohesion.
He expressed concern over the increasing use of political platforms and social media to spread inflammatory narratives, issue threats and manipulate sensitive national issues for political advantage.
The former aide urged the NSA to work with relevant law enforcement agencies to establish and publicly communicate clear standards for political conduct.
He said this was necessary, particularly as the country approaches another competitive political period.
Showunmi, convener of the Alternative Movement, also advocated an early-intervention mechanism to address credible threats, organised intimidation and inflammatory conduct that could endanger public safety.
He maintained that security agencies should act promptly and lawfully on credible evidence rather than wait until provocative statements and threats escalate into violence.
“There is a difference between robust political engagement and conduct that deliberately or recklessly threatens public peace.
“There is a difference between criticising government and deliberately inciting citizens against one another.
“The security and law enforcement agencies must make it clear that no individual is above the law,” he said.
He said any credible evidence of criminal incitement, threats, intimidation or other unlawful conduct must receive appropriate attention.
Showunmi, however, clarified that his appeal was not intended to suppress opposition, silence critical voices or criminalise legitimate political disagreements.
He said democracy must accommodate criticism, protests and competing political opinions while protecting the country against individuals who exploit democratic freedoms to threaten national security.
He urged Ribadu to send a clear message that nobody, irrespective of political position or influence, is above the law.
Showunmi said the country’s security and stability should take precedence over individual political ambitions. (NAN)
Edited by Ijendu Iheaka and Moses Solanke

items.title: Don advocates greater engagements with Islamic schools for religious tolerance

original_payload.original_title: Don advocates greater engagements with Islamic schools for religious tolerance
original_payload.original_body:
General News  Don advocates greater engagements with Islamic schools for religious tolerance
By  Folasade Akpan   ·   4 hours ago   ·  4 min read
✓
✓
​‌‌⁠‍​​‍⁠⁠‍‍‌⁠⁠‌‍‍By Suleiman Shehu
Prof. Afis Oladosu of the Department of Arabic and Islamic Studies, University of Ibadan, has advocated greater engagement with Islamic schools to promote peace and religious tolerance in Nigeria.
Oladosu, the team lead of a research study on “promoting peace and religious co-existence using Arabic and Islamic schools (Ile Kewu) in Ibadan, Nigeria,” stated this at a Dissemination Workshop, on Monday in Ibadan.
The News Agency of Nigeria (NAN) reports that the research was sponsored by International Peace Research Foundation (IPRAF).
The research was initiated to explore how Islamic educational institutions could contribute to building a more peaceful and harmonious society.
The don said that traditional Arabic schools, popularly known as Ile Kewu in Yorubaland and Makaranta in Northern Nigeria, have significant roles to play in shaping attitudes towards peace and interreligious relations in Nigeria.
Oladosu said that the research was motivated by the recognition that traditional Islamic schools could serve as breeding grounds for either peacebuilders or those whose actions could threaten peaceful coexistence, depending on the teachings and values they promote.
He explained that the project sought to review and interpret texts used in traditional Arabic schools in ways that reinforce Islamic teachings on peaceful coexistence, particularly in a religiously diverse society such as Nigeria.
Oladosu disclosed that the research team had undertaken several activities, including visits to selected Arabic schools, interviews with teachers and students, focus group discussions and wider interactive sessions involving both groups.
He said that the information gathered from those engagements provided the foundation for the dissemination workshop in order to present and discuss some of the research findings.
The don stressed that peace must not be taken for granted, saying it requires deliberate, continuous and collective efforts from individuals, religious institutions and society at large.
“If we all desire peace, we have to work for it. We have to strive for it, promote it, talk about it and live it. It is a lifelong exercise,” he said.
Oladosu further warned that the pursuit of peace should never be considered a completed assignment because new threats and factors capable of undermining peaceful coexistence would continue to emerge.
According to him, individuals and institutions committed to peace must remain vigilant and consistently identify and address developments that could threaten social harmony.
The research team lead expressed appreciation to the project’s collaborator, IPRAF, for its support and assistance throughout the research activities.
Also speaking, a member of the research team, Dr Khalid Afolabi, urged Muslim scholars, Arabic teachers and Nigerians in general to make peace a priority in their actions, statements and engagements with others.
Afolabi emphasised that peaceful relationships were beneficial not only to individuals but also to communities and the wider society.
He cautioned Islamic clerics and teachers against careless or inflammatory statements capable of misrepresenting the teachings of Islam and creating negative perceptions of Muslims among people of other faiths.
“Malams and Muslim scholars have to be very mindful and careful of their utterances so that we do not misrepresent Islam or the fundamentals of the faith to outsiders in a way that will make them perceive us as violent people,” he said.
Afolabi maintained that religious leaders and teachers have an important responsibility to ensure their teachings, public statements and interactions reflected the values of peace, tolerance and mutual understanding.
A participant at the workshop, Mr Ibrahim Korede, advocated social media regulations, saying misuse of social media, among other factors, contributed to religious intolerance and violence in the society.
The research highlights the importance of traditional Islamic educational institutions as strategic platforms for promoting peace, strengthening interfaith understanding and addressing attitudes that could contribute to religious intolerance and violence in Nigeria. (NAN)

items.title: 20e Sommet de la Francophonie : Louise Mushikiwabo prolongé de douze mois

original_payload.original_title: 20e Sommet de la Francophonie : Louise Mushikiwabo prolongé de douze mois
original_payload.original_body:
Le 20e Sommet de la Francophonie s’est achevé le 16 novembre 2026 à Phnom Penh, au Cambodge. Les dirigeants ont adopté trois textes sur la paix, les crises internationales et le patrimoine culturel. Ils ont également prolongé de douze mois le mandat de Louise Mushikiwabo.
Les chefs d’État et de gouvernement ont clôturé les travaux après deux jours d’échanges. La rencontre s’est tenue autour du thème : « Réinvestir dans la paix pour une prospérité partagée et une stabilité durable ».
À l’issue des discussions, les participants ont adopté trois documents majeurs. Il s’agit de la Déclaration de Phnom Penh, d’une Résolution sur les situations de crise et de consolidation de la paix. Le troisième texte constitue l’Appel de Phnom Penh pour la protection du patrimoine culturel.
D’abord, la Déclaration de Phnom Penh réaffirme l’engagement des États en faveur de la paix. Elle soutient également les actions de l’Organisation internationale de la Francophonie (OIF). Ces actions concernent notamment l’État de droit, la médiation et l’accompagnement des transitions politiques.
Le document accorde aussi une place importante aux jeunes et aux femmes. Il les considère comme des acteurs essentiels de la consolidation de la paix.
En outre, les dirigeants veulent protéger l’espace informationnel contre les manipulations et les ingérences. Ils souhaitent également placer l’humain au centre du développement de l’intelligence artificielle. Cette ambition implique une participation accrue des pays francophones à la gouvernance numérique mondiale.
Les crises internationales au centre des préoccupations
Sur le plan sécuritaire, la Résolution examine près d’une vingtaine de situations de crise. Elle évoque notamment l’Arménie, le Soudan, Haïti, le Sahel et le Moyen-Orient.
Les dirigeants ont aussi exprimé leurs préoccupations concernant deux foyers de tension. Le premier concerne les tensions frontalières entre le Cambodge et la Thaïlande. Le second porte sur la situation dans l’Est de la République démocratique du Congo (RDC).
À ce sujet, les participants ont salué la mission d’information déployée par la Secrétaire générale. Cette initiative répond à l’appel de la RDC à la solidarité francophone.
Par ailleurs, l’Appel de Phnom Penh engage les États à mieux protéger leur patrimoine culturel. Il prévoit également une lutte renforcée contre le trafic illicite des biens culturels. Les gouvernements devront aussi favoriser la restitution des biens concernés.
Louise Mushikiwabo conserve ses fonctions jusqu’en 2027
La question du renouvellement de la direction de l’OIF a également marqué ce sommet. Les États membres n’ont trouvé aucun consensus sur le choix d’un candidat. Ils ne se sont pas davantage accordés sur la tenue d’un vote.
Face à cette impasse, la présidence cambodgienne a proposé une solution de compromis. Elle consiste à prolonger de douze mois le mandat de Louise Mushikiwabo. Les chefs d’État et de gouvernement ont retenu cette proposition.
La Secrétaire générale restera donc en fonction pendant cette période supplémentaire. Elle devra clarifier les règles électorales pour faciliter l’organisation d’une élection en 2027.
Lors de la cérémonie de clôture, Louise Mushikiwabo a rappelé les réformes engagées depuis 2019. Ces réformes visent à rendre l’organisation plus transparente, efficace et visible. Elle a également réaffirmé son engagement à servir les intérêts de l’institution.
Ottawa accueillera le prochain sommet en 2027
Après Phnom Penh, la Francophonie met le cap sur le Canada. Ottawa accueillera le 21e Sommet de l’organisation en 2027. Un pré-sommet de la jeunesse francophone précédera cette rencontre au Nouveau-Brunswick.
Le Premier ministre canadien, Mark Carney, a annoncé le thème central du prochain rendez-vous. Les échanges porteront sur la découvrabilité des contenus francophones à l’ère de l’intelligence artificielle.
Enfin, le sommet de Phnom Penh a enregistré deux nouvelles admissions au statut d’observateur. Saint-Christophe-et-Niévès et le Manitoba rejoignent désormais l’organisation à ce titre.
L’OIF compte ainsi 92 États et gouvernements. Elle regroupe 53 membres, 5 membres associés et 34 observateurs.

items.title: 20e Sommet de la Francophonie : Fatimé Aldjineh Garfa prend part aux échanges sur la paix et la prospérité partagée

original_payload.original_title: 20e Sommet de la Francophonie : Fatimé Aldjineh Garfa prend part aux échanges sur la paix et la prospérité partagée
original_payload.original_body:
Les travaux du 20e Sommet de la Francophonie se sont poursuivis les 15 et 16 novembre 2026 à Phnom Penh, au Cambodge, avec la tenue des sessions plénières consacrées aux grands enjeux de l’espace francophone.
À cette occasion, Mme  Fatimé Aldjineh Garfa , Ministre déléguée auprès du Ministre d’État, ministre des Affaires étrangères, a pris part aux échanges de haut niveau autour du thème central : « Réinvestir dans la paix pour une prospérité partagée et une stabilité durable ».
Ces sessions plénières ont réuni des chefs d’État et de gouvernement ainsi que leurs représentants, dans un cadre de concertation visant à examiner les défis auxquels sont confrontés les pays de l’espace francophone et à identifier des réponses communes et concertées.
Les discussions ont notamment mis en lumière l’importance de renforcer la coopération entre les États membres, de promouvoir la paix et la stabilité, mais aussi de faire de la solidarité et du dialogue des leviers essentiels pour construire une prospérité durable et inclusive.
La participation de Mme  Fatimé Aldjineh Garfa  à ces travaux témoigne de l’engagement du Tchad à prendre part aux réflexions et aux initiatives portées au sein de la Francophonie, en faveur de la paix, de la coopération internationale et du développement partagé.
À travers ce rendez-vous majeur, les États et gouvernements membres réaffirment leur volonté de faire de l’espace francophone un cadre de dialogue, de solidarité et d’action collective face aux défis contemporains.

items.title: Cargo ship capsizes off Bulgaria’s Black Sea coast

original_payload.original_title: Cargo ship capsizes off Bulgaria’s Black Sea coast
original_payload.original_body:
A cargo ship has capsized off Bulgaria’s Black Sea coast, the country’s Transport Ministry has said.
The ship’s crew, eight Turkish citizens and four Azerbaijani nationals, were rescued from the Somali-flagged Betul 8 in an operation on Monday that involved four ships, two from Bulgaria, one from Romania and one from Turkiye.
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items    list 1 of 3  Russia expels Moldovan diplomat in tit-for-tat move
list 2 of 3  US and rivals spar over next UN boss as race lurches towards deadline
list 3 of 3  At least 12 people killed in Bulgaria motorway pile-up
end of list
Bulgaria’s Transport Ministry confirmed that one of its helicopters repatriated them to shore and that the crew was in good health.
Speaking to journalists after being brought to the port city of Varna, crew members said their ship had been hit by two sea drones.
The incident comes after three ships were hit off Romania over the weekend, according to authorities in Bucharest, though no casualties were reported.
In this photo provided by Varna Regional Administration, a rescue helicopter landed after a rescue operation of Somali-flagged cargo ship sunk in Bulgaria’s Black Sea exclusive economic zone, in Varna, Bulgaria, Monday, November 16, 2026 [Varna Regional Administration via AP]   Romanian Foreign Minister Dan Neculaescu said on Monday the latest incidents were “unacceptable”.
The ship was carrying 3,000 metric tons of wheat and was headed to Egypt from Romania. Bulgaria received a distress signal early on Monday that the ship was sinking approximately 40 nautical miles (74km) southeast of Cape Kaliakra.
Black Sea attacks
Betul 8 is the 17th vessel to be attacked off the coasts of Bulgaria and Romania since mid-July, according to Diaplous, a maritime security firm.

items.title: Israeli court upholds detention of Palestinian land activist Ghassan Najjar

original_payload.original_title: Israeli court upholds detention of Palestinian land activist Ghassan Najjar
original_payload.original_body:
An Israeli military court has upheld a four–month administrative detention order against Palestinian land activist and farmer Ghassan Najjar.
Najjar appeared at Ofer Military Court on Monday. He was arrested during a pre–dawn raid on Burin village, south of Nablus, in the occupied West Bank on October 27, and has been held in  administrative detention  since.
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items    list 1 of 3  Netanyahu may fall, but his far-right legacy in Israel is going nowhere
list 2 of 3  Israel takes measures to crush Palestinian business in occupied West Bank
list 3 of 3  As homes seized, Jericho’s Palestinian residents fear settler takeover
end of list
The Israeli authorities have not given a reason for Najjar’s arrest, as administrative detention allows them. The Palestinian human rights defender, farmer and veteran grassroots organiser has a long history of arrest, having spent nearly a decade in Israeli prisons, much of it under administrative detention. He has been subjected to a travel ban since 2011.
The Institute for Middle East Understanding (IMEU) told Al Jazeera that Najjar was arrested because he intended to harvest olives on his land and planned to help other Palestinian farmers do the same. Israel’s security agency Shin Bet reportedly warned Najjar, cofounder of Burin’s Land and Farming Agricultural Cooperative, that he would be arrested if he did not stop organising with grassroots groups and Western activists.
The olive harvest in the occupied West Bank is a key target of pogroms by Israeli settlers. The attacks have  surged  during this year’s harvest and have already surpassed last year’s figures.
The United Nations and international voices have long urged Israel to guarantee Palestinian farmers’ protection and safe access to their land.
‘Helpless’
Administrative detention allows Israel to detain people without charge or trial, notes B’Tselem, an Israeli human rights group. It adds that the absence of legal proceedings leaves detainees “helpless”.

Tesla and SpaceX CEO Elon Musk and other Silicon Valley insiders are calling on chipmaker Nvidia to reinstate  Jensen Huang,  who resigned last week from the company he cofounded.
Musk is one of the 177,000 signatories  to a petition titled  “Stand With Jensen”, calling for the reinstatement of the executive, who resigned following reports of extramarital affairs, including one with an alleged Chinese spy.

items.title: Iraq deploys army to stronghold of Iran-backed Kataib Hezbollah

original_payload.original_title: Iraq deploys army to stronghold of Iran-backed Kataib Hezbollah
original_payload.original_body:
Iraq has ordered its armed forces to move into a stronghold of the Iran-backed Kataib Hezbollah group, amid an investigation into suspected oil smuggling.
Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi has ordered the military to enter the town of Jurf al-Nasr, government spokesman Haidar al-Aboudi said on Monday, according to the state-run Iraqi News Agency (INA). The Iraqi leader has also set a deadline for the armed faction, which has been implicated in the oil probe, to leave the area.
Recommended Stories
list of 4 items    list 1 of 4  From the UK to the Gulf, are US overseas bases becoming liabilities?
list 2 of 4  Iraq PM sacks nine officials over oil smuggling in pro-Iran stronghold
list 3 of 4  Will Iraq’s oil smuggling crackdown disarm militias without a conflict?
list 4 of 4  Iraqi armed group denies involvement in oil smuggling, calls probe a ‘lie’
end of list
The order comes amid pressure on Baghdad from the United States and some of its Gulf-state allies to counter Tehran’s influence in Iraq.
Al-Aboudi told local media the “deadline is not far off”. A senior Iraqi official told Al Jazeera Arabic that Kataib Hezbollah has until Friday to leave Jurf al-Nasr, which sits south of Baghdad in the centre of the country and was previously known as Jurf al-Sakhar.
Al-Zaidi told military and security commanders to deploy additional forces around the town and to prepare for government troops to enter. The order would potentially bring the government and its troops into direct confrontation with the armed group.
Security agencies have also been instructed to prevent tankers carrying oil or petroleum products from leaving the area.
Iraq recently launched a sweeping anticorruption crackdown centred on the town, which allegedly harbours illicit oil refineries.
Kataib Hezbollah, one of dozens of heavily armed pro-Iranian groups that have semi-official status in Iraq,  denied  the allegations on Sunday, saying that an inspection found no interference with pipelines.

items.title: Iran braces for natural gas shortages during winter energy imbalance

original_payload.original_title: Iran braces for natural gas shortages during winter energy imbalance
original_payload.original_body:
Tehran, Iran –  Iran is heading into winter with warnings of natural gas shortages, as damage from strikes by the United States and Israel deepens an energy imbalance that has plagued the resource-rich country for years.
Iran holds the second-largest proven natural gas reserves in the world, only behind Russia, but its government last week forecast a peak-demand deficit of about 430 million cubic metres per day for winter that could impact both households and industries.
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items    list 1 of 3  Houthis edge closer to Aden as Yemeni forces pull out of Bab al-Mandeb
list 2 of 3  Lebanon’s second airport could provide economic and political benefits
list 3 of 3  USS Roosevelt arrives in Middle East: Is the US-Iran war about to resume?
end of list
The country’s ageing energy infrastructure has long suffered from underinvestment and international sanctions that have restricted finances and equipment. Authorities say that inefficient consumption and limited storage capacity are also to blame, in addition to the damage from the ongoing war.
Saeed Tavakoli, head of the National Iranian Gas Company, told local media last week that 26 projectiles struck six refineries on March 18, knocking out 28 percent of Iran’s gas production capacity in the immediate aftermath of the strikes.
According to the government, about 100 million cubic metres per day of processing capacity has since been restored, but fully bringing back the additional 130 million cubic metres lost in the US and Israeli attacks could extend into 2028.
Hashem Oraee, head of the Iranian Energy Associations Union, told local media last week that Iran was not able to rely on any gas imports to plug the gap.
Gas shortages could also lead to electricity blackouts if the gas feeding some power plants goes out, something that has repeatedly happened in recent years. To avoid electricity shortages, those power plants  resort to burning cheap fuel , predominantly a heavy oil alternative called mazut, which significantly pollutes the air.

items.title: At least 17 killed in two South Africa mass shootings

original_payload.original_title: At least 17 killed in two South Africa mass shootings
original_payload.original_body:
At least 17 people have been killed in two separate mass shootings in South Africa, police said.
Eight men were found dead late on Sunday in a “bullet-riddled” vehicle in Sweetwaters, outside the city of Pietermaritzburg, police said.
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items    list 1 of 3  More than 900 arrested during South Africa’s antimigrant protests
list 2 of 3  At least 11 people killed in South Africa township shooting
list 3 of 3  Dozens killed in two mass shootings in South Africa
end of list
Hours later, nine people were found dead in Jeffsville, an informal settlement near South Africa’s capital, Pretoria, police said. The bodies of six men and three women were discovered inside a shack with gunshot wounds.
National Police Commissioner Fannie Masemola said on Monday that investigators had not established motives for the crimes that took place 530 kilometres (330 miles) apart.
“The ongoing mass shootings which we encounter are unacceptable. Definitely, we have to find these criminals. We cannot allow them to terrorise communities or determine how people live their lives,” Masemola said.
Surge in deadly shootings
South Africa has struggled for years with high rates of violent crime, but has had a recent surge in mass shootings with high death tolls.
Reporting from Pretoria, Al Jazeera’s Clement Manyathela said the community was “gripped by fear” as it waits for answers about the shooting.
He said the victims were found in a four-room shack, where the killings happened just before midnight. A young child who went into the shack looking for a relative made the discovery, he said.
Pathologists, investigators and officers were working to establish what happened.
Gauteng Police Commissioner Tommy Mthombeni said one of those killed was a “person of interest” in a shooting last year in the nearby informal settlement of Saulsville, in which 12 people were killed and 13 wounded, the Associated Press news agency reported.

items.title: Why Starshield limits are hurting Ukraine against jet-powered drones

original_payload.original_title: Why Starshield limits are hurting Ukraine against jet-powered drones
original_payload.original_body:
Ukraine’s President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has warned that limits on SpaceX’s  Starshield  military-grade internet service are disrupting Ukrainian drone operations and hindering the country’s war effort against Russia.
Over the weekend, two people were killed in a Russian jet-powered drone attack on what Ukrainian officials called “critical infrastructure” in the northern Koriukivka region. An energy facility was also hit in Odesa overnight on Sunday, leaving 41,000 households without electricity.
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items    list 1 of 3  US envoy Kushner says he aims to broker Europe-Russia talks on Ukraine
list 2 of 3  Give Donbas, take NATO seat: Could new US pitch work for Ukraine, Russia?
list 3 of 3  Starshield restrictions help Russia’s energy attacks on Ukraine: Zelenskyy
end of list
Zelenskyy linked the success of these Russian strikes to limits that he said had been placed on Ukraine’s use of Starshield. The country’s military has been relying on the service since December 2024 to intercept Russian drones.
Starshield is a sister service to Starlink, a network of 11,000 satellites launched into low Earth orbit by SpaceX  to provide high-speed internet connectivity, even in remote areas.
What did Zelenskyy say?
In a  statement  on X on Sunday, Zelenskyy said that Russia was targeting energy substations with Shahed drones, which both sides often use to attack each other.
He added that “many of these strikes are getting through because restrictions on the operating speed of Starshield terminals along the front line and in the temporarily occupied territories are still there”.
“We are counting on these restrictions being lifted. The protection of lives and Ukraine’s energy infrastructure ahead of winter directly depends on this,” he added.
Zelenskyy also accused Starlink’s sister service of throttling internet speeds and hampering military operations on Saturday. He said that the internet restrictions had been in place for five days.
