items.title: Conflicts, Economic Uncertainty and Climate Pressures Dominate International Agenda

original_payload.original_title: Conflicts, Economic Uncertainty and Climate Pressures Dominate International Agenda
original_payload.original_body:
By Staff Writer
November 15 , 2026 (ENA)
The week of November 9–15, 2026, underscored the growing complexity of the international landscape, as geopolitical tensions, economic uncertainty, humanitarian emergencies and climate challenges continued to shape global affairs. Developments across the Middle East, Eastern Europe and Southeast Asia highlighted how conflicts, economic pressures and environmental risks increasingly transcend national borders, reinforcing the need for stronger international cooperation and coordinated responses.
From persistent security tensions and shifting trade dynamics to climate negotiations and emerging technological risks, the week's developments reflected an international system facing multiple, interconnected challenges.
Regional Conflicts and International Stability
Geopolitical tensions remained a major concern for international peace and security, with the wars in Ukraine and the Middle East continuing to command global attention.
In Ukraine, continued attacks on electricity infrastructure heightened concerns over civilian access to heating, electricity and other essential services as winter approached. The situation underscored the vulnerability of critical infrastructure during armed conflict and the broader humanitarian consequences of prolonged hostilities.
Meanwhile, tensions involving Iran and the wider Middle East continued to carry implications for regional security and global energy markets. The strategic importance of the Strait of Hormuz, through which a substantial share of internationally traded oil passes, made the potential disruption of maritime transportation a persistent concern for energy-importing economies.
In Southeast Asia, the ASEAN Summit in Manila placed regional security and Myanmar's prolonged political crisis high on the diplomatic agenda. Discussions also addressed tensions in the South China Sea, where competing territorial claims and strategic interests continued to test regional cooperation. Despite diplomatic initiatives, differences over political legitimacy, sovereignty and security remained significant obstacles to lasting stability.
Global Economic Developments
The global economy continued to navigate a challenging environment shaped by inflationary pressures, monetary policy uncertainty and shifting international trade patterns.
In the United States, persistent inflation complicated expectations surrounding Federal Reserve monetary policy. The prospect of interest rates remaining elevated raised concerns about international borrowing costs, investment flows and financial conditions, particularly for developing economies already facing debt and financing pressures.
China, meanwhile, recorded strong trade performance in October. According to the International Monetary Fund's November 10 Global Markets Monitor, exports increased by 35.2 percent year-on-year, while imports rose by 41.6 percent. High-technology exports expanded by 66.6 percent, highlighting the growing importance of advanced manufacturing in China's global trade position.
The country's year-to-date trade surplus also exceeded one trillion US dollars, underscoring its continued influence on international commerce and global supply chains.
Meanwhile, oil prices faced downward pressure amid expectations of diplomatic progress in the Middle East. Nevertheless, the possibility of disruptions to shipping through the Strait of Hormuz continued to expose the global economy to energy-supply risks, demonstrating the close relationship between geopolitical developments and economic stability.
Climate Diplomacy and COP31
Climate change remained a major international priority, with the 31st United Nations Climate Change Conference (COP31), held in Antalya, Türkiye, providing a central platform for negotiations on emissions reduction, climate finance, renewable energy and adaptation.
Developing countries, particularly African nations and vulnerable island states, renewed calls for predictable and accessible climate financing, technology transfer and stronger international support to address the growing impacts of climate change.
On November 14, UN Climate Change Executive Secretary Simon Stiell urged negotiators to accelerate discussions, warning that wars, inflation and competing international crises risked pushing climate action down governments' political priorities.
The conference also highlighted the persistent gap between existing national climate commitments and the measures required to keep the global temperature increase within the 1.5-degree Celsius threshold.
Among the initiatives discussed were Türkiye's global electrification proposal and efforts to mobilize more than one billion US dollars for resilience programmes benefiting 14 island economies.
For Africa, COP31 represented an important opportunity to advance priorities extending beyond emissions reduction to include climate justice, adaptation financing, renewable energy development, sustainable agriculture and forest conservation. The continent's position remained particularly important given its limited contribution to historical global emissions and disproportionate exposure to climate-related risks.
Democracy, Governance and Regional Cooperation
Democratic governance and regional political stability remained central to discussions in Southeast Asia, particularly amid the prolonged crisis in Myanmar.
At the ASEAN Summit, the limited progress in implementing the bloc's five-point peace framework highlighted the difficulties regional institutions face in addressing protracted political conflicts. The situation continued to raise questions about the effectiveness of regional diplomatic mechanisms in promoting political dialogue, reconciliation and stability.
At the same time, tensions in the South China Sea demonstrated the importance of sustained diplomatic engagement and regional cooperation in managing competing territorial and maritime interests.
These developments reinforced the need for effective multilateral institutions capable of addressing political disagreements while safeguarding regional peace, sovereignty and international law.
Humanitarian Emergencies and Civilian Protection
Humanitarian emergencies continued to deepen the vulnerability of populations affected by conflict and extreme weather.
In Gaza, heavy rainfall damaged temporary shelters and essential infrastructure, worsening already difficult living conditions for displaced families. A UN humanitarian situation report issued on November 13 indicated that more than 46,000 households had been affected by flooding and shelter damage, underscoring the urgent need for humanitarian assistance and improved protection for vulnerable communities.
In Ukraine, continued attacks on electricity infrastructure threatened access to heating, healthcare, water and other essential services as temperatures declined.
Together, these developments illustrated how armed conflict and extreme weather can compound humanitarian crises, particularly where infrastructure has already been weakened and populations have limited access to basic necessities. They reinforced the importance of sustained humanitarian access, civilian protection and international assistance in accordance with international humanitarian law.
Technology, Artificial Intelligence and International Security
The rapid advancement of emerging technologies, particularly artificial intelligence and autonomous weapons systems, added another important dimension to international security discussions.
The United Nations Convention on Certain Conventional Weapons was preparing for its Seventh Review Conference in Geneva, scheduled for November 16–20. Governments were expected to consider further steps toward developing international rules governing autonomous weapons systems.
Growing concerns over accountability, civilian protection and compliance with international humanitarian law have intensified as artificial intelligence becomes increasingly integrated into military operations and weapons technologies.
Beyond security applications, AI is also reshaping economic competitiveness, public administration, scientific research and international trade. Its expanding influence presents both opportunities and challenges, particularly for developing countries seeking to participate in the emerging digital economy.
For these countries, investment in digital infrastructure, education, research, skills development and local innovation will be essential to narrowing technological gaps and ensuring that the benefits of digital transformation are more widely shared.
Africa and the Global South: Shared Challenges, Common Priorities
The week's international developments further highlighted the interconnected challenges confronting Africa and the wider Global South, including mounting debt pressures, climate vulnerability, food insecurity, infrastructure financing gaps and unequal access to international markets. For African economies, strengthening regional integration, expanding productive capacity and improving transport and energy infrastructure remain essential to achieving sustainable growth and greater economic resilience.
The African Continental Free Trade Area (AfCFTA) offers a significant opportunity to expand intra-African trade, strengthen industrial cooperation and create a more integrated continental market. However, realizing its full potential will require continued investment in infrastructure, efficient customs systems, trade facilitation and domestic productive capacity.
Climate finance also remained a critical priority. COP31 provided African countries with an important platform to press for more accessible financing, technology transfer and international partnerships to support renewable energy, agricultural modernization, forest conservation and climate adaptation.
Beyond these immediate priorities, the broader challenge for the Global South is to secure a more equitable role in international economic and political decision-making, ensuring that global responses to shared challenges reflect the interests and development needs of all countries.
Conclusion: The Case for Stronger Global Cooperation
The developments of November 9–15 demonstrated that international security, economic stability, humanitarian protection, climate action and technological advancement are increasingly interconnected.
Continuing conflicts in Ukraine and the Middle East highlighted the urgent need for sustained diplomatic engagement and civilian protection. Economic developments in the United States and China illustrated how the policies and performance of major economies influence global trade, financial conditions and developing countries. Meanwhile, COP31 brought renewed attention to the unresolved questions of climate responsibility and financing, while discussions on autonomous weapons underscored the growing importance of international technology governance.
Taken together, the week's developments point to a central challenge facing the international community: addressing global crises not as isolated events, but as interconnected problems requiring coordinated and forward-looking solutions.
Strengthening multilateral institutions, revitalizing diplomatic mechanisms, promoting inclusive economic growth and ensuring equitable access to climate finance and emerging technologies will be essential to building a more stable, resilient and sustainable international order.

items.title: Africa: The End of a Cancer Is in Sight for the First Time in Public Health History

original_payload.original_title: Africa: The End of a Cancer Is in Sight for the First Time in Public Health History
original_payload.original_body:
To mark Tuesday’s World Cervical Cancer Elimination Day, global health leaders highlight the progress achieved and prospects of consigning cervical cancer to the annals of history.
For the first time in public health history, the end of a cancer is in sight.  We already have the tools to make this possible. With HPV (human papilloma virus) vaccination, screening and timely treatment, cervical cancer could become the first cancer ever eliminated.
Each year more than 600,000 women are diagnosed with cervical cancer and about 280,000 lose their lives. Behind every number is a woman whose life, family and future matters. When a mother dies, her children will be left to grow up without her love, protection and support. These maternal orphans are among the often-invisible victims of cervical cancer, their loss echoing across families, communities and generations.
Women in the world’s poorest places are the most affected.

items.title: Sudan: Sudan's State Collapse - Canary in the Coal Mine for International Peace and Security

original_payload.original_title: Sudan: Sudan's State Collapse - Canary in the Coal Mine for International Peace and Security
original_payload.original_body:
Sudan's harrowing state implosion since war resumed in 2023 presents a warning for other states in Africa and elsewhere currently heading in that direction as well as stark dilemmas for U.S. foreign policy.
Just as Somalia's state collapse provided an instructive example in the 1990s, Sudan is experiencing a much more consequential slide into a country where multiple international security and peace threats emerge, from  chemical weapons  to interconnected conflicts throughout a broad regional swathe to the world's most devastating humanitarian crisis. Sudan's state collapse is a canary in the coal mine for similar countries at risk from Libya to Lebanon to Haiti to multiple neighbors, first and foremost  South Sudan .
Sudan's collapse is a canary in the coal mine for countries at risk from Libya to Lebanon to Haiti to multiple neighbors.
At a moment when there are  more simultaneous conflicts  globally since WWII, Sudan's war stands out in its size and scope.  The numbers are staggering.  It is the world's largest displacement crisis, with  14 million people  rendered homeless by the violence.  It is the world's  largest  hunger crisis, with  40% of the country's population  facing acute food insecurity.  And it is  arguably  the world's  largest sexual violence crisis .  The UN's Tom Fletcher  concluded , "Sudan is an atrocities laboratory: sieges, denial of food, weaponized sexual violence…"
As the fighting rages on, the crisis only will metastasize, as fertilizer and fuel  shortages  due to the Iran conflict increase the cost of food, thus driving millions more into extreme hunger.
The funding gaps are gaping, with UNICEF, the World Food Program, and the UN High Commission for Refugees all facing shortfalls between  70 and 85  percent of assessed needs.  That directly translates into more starving kids, more virulent epidemics, etc.
The roots of Sudan's collapse share commonalities with other states in extreme distress.
Sudan's case is extreme but not isolated.  The roots of its collapse share commonalities with several other states in extreme distress.
First, state capture .  For decades, Sudan's rulers and their external collaborators have hijacked state institutions for private gain, creating a classic  violent kleptocracy.   A coalition of thieves of state ruled the country, and then fell out over its spoils, as thieves do, tearing the country apart in the process.  The worst abuser of human rights, the genocidal militia known as the Rapid Support Forces (RSF), was originally a collection of racist militias known as the  Janjaweed , subsequently organized by Sudan's long-time dictator Omer al-Bashir to fight an incipient rebellion in Darfur.  Unsurprisingly, as those militias grew in power and acquired greater wealth, they  turned  on their former government benefactors and made a play for raw power, leading to massive civil war, total state collapse, and the possible further partitioning of the country.
Second, resource extraction .  Sudan's rich resources, particularly oil and gold, have been pillaged by successive governments, allied militias, rebel groups, and unscrupulous external actors.  Parasitic multinational networks have created an assembly line of violently extracted and smuggled raw materials in Sudan and many other failing states, enriching a handful of insiders and outsiders while the communities and countries are ravaged economically and environmentally.  The result is  war as an economic system  fueled by resource extraction, smuggling,  checkpoint  taxation, and the fleecing of humanitarian aid efforts.  In Sudan and other African states such as the Democratic Republic of Congo, South Sudan, and the Central African Republic, the global acceleration in the price of gold has led to ever more violent contestations over control of the mining and trafficking of  conflict gold ,  particularly  to the United Arab Emirates (UAE). The UAE  imports  well over $1 billion worth of illicit gold from Sudan per year.
Third, environmental poisoning .  As part of the gold rush in Sudan and many other countries, increased artisanal mining is contributing to  public health emergencies  resulting from chemicals poisoning the groundwater, soil, and communities surrounding the mines.  Agricultural communities near the mines in River Nile state now say that crop production has decreased by up to  80% to 90%  due to toxic chemicals used in gold mining.
Fourth, external intervention.   The Cold War construct of the United States versus the Soviet Union has been replaced in Sudan by a raging rivalry between the UAE backing the RSF and Saudi Arabia, Egypt, Turkey, Iran, and Russia backing the rival Sudan Armed Forces.  At a recent international donors' conference in Berlin on the Sudan crisis, the UAE and Saudi Arabia  tanked  the joint communique because the Emirates couldn't even agree to the Saudi insistence on preserving "state institutions."  The rise of the so-called Middle Powers has created a more complex chessboard in war-torn states from the Democratic Republic of Congo to Yemen where external actors pour in arms and/or trade  in conflict resources such as gold  with no consequences, as they pursue conflicting agendas related to influence and resources that make mediation efforts much more challenging.
Fifth, weapons systems . Provided by Iran, Egypt, Türkiye, and especially the UAE to the belligerents,  attack drones  have become the weapon of choice in Sudan, representative of a trend also seen in conflicts as far afield as Iran, Ukraine, and Mali.  The use of these drones has completely changed the nature of warfare.  The usual ebb and flow of conflict related to seasonal rains has been rendered moot; attacks on civilian targets can be mounted from further away with deadly accuracy.  The cost of a quick and dirty "offensive" can be minimal for the attacker, but devastating for the target, usually civilian.  Recently, there has been a  surge of drone attacks  on food distribution efforts, which ties drone strikes directly to increased starvation. Even more alarmingly for international security, the Sudan Armed Forces were recently found to be  using chemical weapons —chlorine gas bombs—in violation of international arms treaties.

items.title: Africa: Facebook Exposure Is Behavioral Intelligence - Not Vanity Metrics

original_payload.original_title: Africa: Facebook Exposure Is Behavioral Intelligence - Not Vanity Metrics
original_payload.original_body:
In March 2026, as Nigeria implemented its measles-rubella vaccination campaign, the World Health Organization ( WHO )  Africa Infodemic Response Alliance  was  listening to what happened online . It revealed how people were receiving, questioning and interpreting the intervention in real-time.
This demonstrates why public health must take social media seriously as a source of behavioral intelligence to inform interventions. Today, people socialize, trade, network, find love and seek information on social media. Public health must meet people where they already are. As of April 2026, there were an  estimated 5.79 billion social media user  identities worldwide, equivalent to about 70% of the global population.
To be sure, social media metrics cannot prove behavior change, but that does not make them "vanity metrics." When interpreted carefully, they can provide valuable behavioral intelligence about how people encounter and respond to an intervention.

items.title: Mozambique: Regulating Smarter - How Mozambique's Tobacco Control Bill Can Protect Public Health, Farmers and the Economy

original_payload.original_title: Mozambique: Regulating Smarter - How Mozambique's Tobacco Control Bill Can Protect Public Health, Farmers and the Economy
original_payload.original_body:
Mozambique is right to modernize its tobacco control framework. The 2007 law was written before products that do not burn tobacco existed. The Tobacco Control Bill is a chance to align the law with today's science and with international practice. But regulation based on evidence has to do more than lower smoking rates. It also has to weigh what each measure means for the farmers, retailers and workers who depend on the sector, and for the public revenues it generates.
Starting from the science
The evidence points to one distinction in particular. Most of the harm from smoking comes from combustion, so non-combusted products are better for adult smokers who would otherwise keep smoking. The Bill would reflect this if it recognized two categories within the definition of tobacco products: combusted tobacco products and smokeless alternatives.

original_payload.original_title: Eritrea: Eritrea Eliminates Trachoma - a Major Public Health Milestone
original_payload.original_body:
The World Health Organization (WHO) has validated Eritrea's elimination of trachoma as a public health problem, making it the 11th country in WHO's African Region and the 34th globally to reach this major milestone.
"I congratulate the Government and people of Eritrea on this historic achievement," said Dr Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, WHO Director-General. "After two decades of determined effort, Eritrea has consigned trachoma as a public health problem to history. This is a victory for the communities most affected by this devastating disease, and a powerful example of what sustained national commitment can achieve."

Ten media organisations have permanently reserved seats including the Portuguese agency LUSA; five more press sets will rotate on a daily basis. The defendant, Mondlane, has 15 seats. The Bar Association will have two reserved seats. Only 10 seats will be available to the general public, rotating and subject to prior registration. Nhatitima said “we will be using a new recording and transcription system. Image and sound recording, followed by transcription into a written document. This helps to significantly reduce the length of the trial.” Previous big trials were written by hand and the text read out.

items.title: Africa: Africa CDC and Canada Deepen Partnership to Strengthen Africa's Defences Against Health Threats

original_payload.original_title: Africa: Africa CDC and Canada Deepen Partnership to Strengthen Africa's Defences Against Health Threats
original_payload.original_body:
New agreement aims to strengthen outbreak detection, laboratory capacity, emergency response and scientific cooperation across the continent.
ADDIS ABABA, Ethiopi  a, 15 November 2026  - The Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention (Africa CDC) and the Public Health Agency of Canada (PHAC) have signed a Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) to deepen cooperation on disease prevention, preparedness and response, as Africa works to strengthen its ability to address current and emerging health threats.
The agreement, signed by H.E. Dr Jean Kaseya, Director General of Africa CDC, and Ms Nancy Hamzawi, President of the Public Health Agency of Canada, establishes a framework for closer technical cooperation, knowledge exchange and joint initiatives in key areas of public health.
Five priority areas of cooperation
The agreement provides a framework for cooperation across five priority areas: epidemiological surveillance and public health intelligence; laboratory systems, biosafety and biosecurity; public health emergency preparedness and response; public health workforce development; and research, innovation and medical countermeasures.
In a context of recurring disease outbreaks, growing cross-border health risks and increasing pressure on health systems, the agreement reflects a shared commitment to strengthening Africa's capacity to detect threats early, respond effectively and invest in the institutions and expertise needed for long-term health security.
"Africa's health security is interconnected with global health security. The ongoing Ebola outbreak on our continent is a powerful reminder that emerging infectious disease threats do not respect borders and that preparedness, scientific collaboration and rapid response are shared global responsibilities. They also demonstrate why strong public health institutions, laboratory networks, epidemiological intelligence and a skilled health workforce are so critical ," said  Dr Jean Kaseya, Director General of Africa CDC .
" I commend the Public Health Agency of Canada for their leadership and commitment to national and global health security. This partnership is therefore not simply about technical cooperation with Africa, but about building a mutually beneficial relationship between Africa and Canada in addressing public health challenges.

items.title: South Africa: #lge2026 - What Happens When No Party Wins? a Guide to Coalitions

original_payload.original_title: South Africa: #lge2026 - What Happens When No Party Wins? a Guide to Coalitions
original_payload.original_body:
#LGE2026: what happens when no party wins? A guide to coalitions
On 4 November 2026, South Africa voted in local government elections to choose new municipal leaders. For the first time,  most of these races  - 138 out of 213 - ended with no party winning a majority of council seats. These "hung councils" are becoming  more common , and  analysts  had predicted this outcome  for months . When this happens, South Africa's electoral system allows parties to form coalitions to govern together.
The phrase "coalition government" might bring to mind the  Government of National Unity  that took power after South Africa's first democratic elections, or its younger namesake  formed after the 2024 general elections . Or perhaps you think of municipal coalitions, like the one that  has run the City of Johannesburg  since 2021, and  its drawn-out struggle to choose a mayor . There has been a  similar challenge in the City of Tshwane .

Nicolas Jackson was on target again as Senegal, Cameroon and Benin moved to the brink of qualification for the 2027 Africa Cup of Nations (Afcon) with away victories.
After Aston Villa striker Jackson had opened the scoring, Senegal gave up a 2-0 lead against Sudan before two late goals sealed a 4-2 win, while five-time Afcon winners Cameroon cruised to a 3-0 triumph over Namibia.
A goal in second-half stoppage time from Ede Oloko sealed a 1-0 success for Benin against Central African Republic.
All three sides are on 10 points in their respective groups after four rounds of matches and will progress to next year's finals in Kenya, Tanzania and Uganda if other results go their way on Tuesday.
Elsewhere, Jordan Ayew's first-half penalty was enough for Ghana to register back-to-back victories over Somalia in Group C.
The Black Stars had home advantage for what should have been an away tie, with the game played in Sekondi-Takoradi because the Ocean Stars do not have a stadium fit for international football.
Ayew had a penalty saved as  Ghana beat Somalia 2-0 in the reverse fixture  last Thursday, but the Sheffield United forward kept his composure when he sent the goalkeeper the wrong way in the 36th minute after Brandon Thomas-Asante had been pulled down in the box.
Ghana, who parted company with Carlos Queiroz after losing their opening two fixtures, move level in the table with The Gambia, with both sides on six points.
Salah scores twice as Egypt and Nigeria win Afcon 2027 qualifiers
Published
3 days ago
Why has Caf abandoned plans to hold Afcon every four years?
Published
30 October
The Gambians are themselves three points adrift of group leaders Ivory Coast before they host the Elephants on Tuesday.
Meanwhile, Guinea moved to the top of Group D after Yakhouba Barry scored twice in their 3-1 away win over Eritrea in neutral Cairo.
The West Africans lead South Africa, who travel to Kenya on Tuesday, by two points in a group with only one qualification spot available because the Kenyans are assured of a spot at the finals as co-hosts.
And Zimbabwe beat Equatorial Guinea 3-0 in Harare to go two points behind Group E table toppers DR Congo.
Thando Ngwenya, Tawanda Chirewa and Tawanda Maswanhise were all on target for the Warriors before Equatorial Guinea's Josete Miranda had a penalty saved and Saul Coco was sent off for the visitors late on.
The National Thunder were without first choice goalkeeper Jesus Owono after  he asked not to be selected  following his involvement in a collision with Tenerife striker Jesus de Miguel, who died the day after the incident.
DR Congo, Ivory Coast, Mali and Morocco can all book their tickets to the tournament when the fourth round of fixtures culminates with 18 matches on Tuesday.
The final two rounds of qualifiers will be held in March next year, with Afcon 2027 scheduled to be held in East Africa from 19 June to 17 July.
Teranga Lions leave it late
Patrick Vieira's  Senegal  survived a scare in neutral Juba after Jackson's early goal put the Teranga Lions ahead and a low strike from Brentford left-back El Hadji Malick Diouf made it 2-0 midway through the first half.
Sudan hit back through Al-Gozoli Nooh and Salah Adel to level proceedings with 15 minutes to play, but Pathe Mboup's lob made it 3-2 in the 87th minute and Paul Mendy made the points safe for the West Africans in the first minute of added time.
Senegal are still awaiting  the outcome of their appeal to the Court of Arbitration for Sport  over the destination of the 2025 Afcon title.
The Teranga Lions beat Morocco 1-0 after extra time in January's final, but a Confederation of African Football appeals board stripped them of the title two months later, decreeing Senegal had breached competition regulations by leaving the field of play in second-half stoppage time in protest at a penalty awarded against them.
Mahamadou Nagida opened the scoring for  Cameroon  against Namibia in neutral Botswana with a stunning volley from outside the box in the 12th minute, and Ryan Fosso's deflected effort doubled the lead just before the hour mark.
Saidou Alioum made it 3-0 with a fine first-time volley with 19 minutes remaining, and David Pagou's men will be assured of a place at Afcon 2027 if Congo-Brazzaville fail to beat Comoros on Tuesday.

items.title: Guinée: 22 ex-administrateurs territoriaux condamnés à deux ans de prison dans l'affaire d'orpaillage illégal à Siguiri

original_payload.original_title: Guinée: 22 ex-administrateurs territoriaux condamnés à deux ans de prison dans l'affaire d'orpaillage illégal à Siguiri
original_payload.original_body:
Guinée: 22 ex-administrateurs territoriaux condamnés à deux ans de prison dans l'affaire d'orpaillage illégal à Siguiri
Jugés devant la Cour de répression des infractions économiques et financières (Crief) pour leur complicité présumée dans l'exploitation minière clandestine qui a débouché sur une catastrophe écologique à Siguiri, ils ont été reconnus coupables de complicité de dégradation de l'environnement, destructions diverses et pollution des eaux. Les 202 orpailleurs également poursuivis dans ce dossier ont quant à eux été condamnés à trois ans de prison et à une amende solidaire de 10 milliards de francs guinéens.
Publié le :  17/11/2026 - 04:40
2 min     Temps de lecture
Les ex-administrateurs territoriaux (en orange) de la région de Siguiri et, derrière eux, les 202 orpailleurs également poursuivis dans ce dossier lors d'une audience devant la Crief, le 11 novembre dernier, à Conakry.        © Mouctar Bah / RFI
Par :
RFI
Publicité
Avec notre correspondant à Conakry,   Mouctar Bah
Le verdict est tombé au procès des 224 individus poursuivis devant la Cour de répression des infractions économiques et financières (Crief) dans le cadre de l'affaire de l'exploitation minière clandestine de Siguiri qui a débouché sur un désastre écologique, dans le nord-est du pays, lundi 16 novembre.
Les 202 orpailleurs reconnus coupables d'exploitation illégale de substances minières et d'atteinte à l’environnement ont été condamnés à trois ans de prison assortis d'une amende solidaire de 10 milliards de francs guinéens - l'équivalent d'environ un million d’euros - et de 10 ans d'interdiction de séjour en   Guinée   pour les ressortissants étrangers concernés.
Quant aux 22 anciens administrateurs territoriaux eux aussi dans le collimateur de la justice, s'ils ont été relaxés des accusations de corruption, d'enrichissement illicite et de blanchiment de capitaux, ils écopent chacun en revanche de deux ans de prison ferme et d'une amende de 10 millions de francs guinéens pour complicité de dégradation de l'environnement, destructions diverses et pollution des eaux.
À peine prononcé, ce verdict a immédiatement suscité des réactions contrastées. D'un côté, le parquet spécial s'en est déclaré satisfait, tandis que les avocats de la défense ont annoncé vouloir consulter leurs clients avant de décider d'un éventuel recours.
Alors que dans la salle d'audience, l'émotion était palpable avec des proches des accusés en larmes, ce procès se referme en soulevant aussi une question de fond : celle de la protection durable de l'environnement face à l'exploitation minière clandestine.
À lire aussi  Orpaillage à Siguiri: face à la justice, l’ex-gouverneur nie toute responsabilité dans les dégâts environnementaux

items.title: Niger: la communauté arabe Mahamid sommée de quitter le pays avant la fin de l'année

original_payload.original_title: Niger: la communauté arabe Mahamid sommée de quitter le pays avant la fin de l'année
original_payload.original_body:
Niger: la communauté arabe Mahamid sommée de quitter le pays avant la fin de l'année
La communauté arabe Mahamid est sommée de quitter le territoire du Niger avant la fin de l'année 2026. Les arabes Mahamid sont plusieurs milliers dans le pays, principalement dans le Sud-Est, souvent depuis plusieurs décennies. Les premiers sont arrivés dans les années 1970, en provenance du Tchad et du Soudan. Cela fait plusieurs mois que les autorités nigériennes prennent des mesures à leur encontre. Des voix s'élèvent pour dénoncer de graves discriminations.
Publié le :  17/11/2026 - 04:39   Modifié le :  17/11/2026 - 04:39
2 min     Temps de lecture
Des membres de la communauté arabe Mahamid creusant une tombe dans le cmap de N'Gortogole, dans l'attente de leur expulsion par les autorités nigériennes, le 27 octobre 2006. (image d'illustration)        AFP - PIUS UTOMI EKPEI
Par :
RFI
Publicité
L'histoire semble se répéter pour les Mahamid du Niger.   Vingt ans après avoir été ciblée   sous la présidence de Mamadou Tandja, la communauté est de nouveau sommée de quitter le territoire nigérien. Ses membres ont jusqu'au 31 décembre 2026 pour s'exécuter. Cet ultimatum a encore été répété, il y a deux jours, à leurs représentants, à Chetimari, dans la région de Diffa.
Ces derniers mois, selon un document imputé au ministère de l'Intérieur, des mesures avaient déjà été prises contre les Mahamid, telles que le retrait des pièces d'état civil nigériennes ou la demande de fermeture des écoles et forages d'eau potable devenus profitables exclusivement à cette communauté, accusées par les autorités du   Niger   de fournir des armes aux groupes armés du bassin du lac Tchad.
À lire aussi  Les habitants du lac Tchad enserrés entre la montée des eaux et Boko Haram
Une politique qui attire les critiques des défenseurs des   droits humains  , qui dénoncent de graves discriminations. «  Les  ''fautes''  commises par quelques individus indélicats ne sauraient justifier, en aucun cas, une mesure collective d'expulsion  », écrit par exemple Mamane Kaka Touda, de l'ONG Alternative espaces citoyens. De son côté, la Commission africaine des droits de l'homme et des peuples a écrit au général   Abdourahamane Tiani  , il y a une dizaine de jours. Elle évoque des «  violations présumées des droits fondamentaux  » des Mahamid dans la région de Diffa.
À lire aussi  L'Algérie envoie des troupes au Niger pour développer son influence au Sahel

items.title: Gabon: l’ancien ministre et ancien commandant en chef de la police Jean-Boniface Assélé placé sous mandat de dépôt

original_payload.original_title: Gabon: l’ancien ministre et ancien commandant en chef de la police Jean-Boniface Assélé placé sous mandat de dépôt
original_payload.original_body:
Gabon: l’ancien ministre et ancien commandant en chef de la police Jean-Boniface Assélé placé sous mandat de dépôt
Celui-ci est accusé d'avoir tiré sur des adolescents qui jouaient sur un terrain de football dont il est le propriétaire, vendredi 13 novembre. L'un d'entre eux nommé Midioko Jayson Merlin Dylan a été admis en soins intensifs après avoir été grièvement blessé au flanc droit.
Publié le :  17/11/2026 - 04:38
1 min     Temps de lecture
Sur les réseaux sociaux gabonais, le fait divers qui a failli tourner au drame a immédiatement suscité de nombreux posts assortis du hashtag : « Justice pour Dylan ».        AFP - -
Par :
RFI
Publicité
Avec notre correspondant à Libreville,   Yves-Laurent Goma
L'incident, qui a failli tourner au drame, suscite une vive émotion au   Gabon  . Vendredi 13 novembre, l’ancien ministre et ancien commandant en chef de la police gabonaise Jean-Boniface Assélé a ouvert le feu sur des adolescents qui jouaient sur un terrain football dont il est le propriétaire.
Arrivé sur place avec son fils, ce dernier aurait fait usage d'un fusil de type calibre 16 après les avoir sommés de quitter les lieux, blessant grièvement au flanc droit un jeune garçon nommé Midioko Jayson Merlin Dylan, selon le procureur de la République Dick Fabrice Boungou Mikolo.
« Justice pour Dylan »
Admis en soins intensifs, cet élève en classe de 3e serait désormais hors de danger, même si une balle se trouve toujours dans son corps à un endroit très sensible, affirme l’équipe médicale.
Sur les réseaux sociaux, la nouvelle a immédiatement suscité de nombreux posts assortis du hashtag « Justice pour Dylan ».
Le président de la République Brice Clotaire Oligui Nguema, qui s’est rendu au chevet de la victime lundi 16 novembre, a affirmé à cette occasion que la justice était la même pour tous. Au même moment, le général Assélé était, lui, présenté au parquet qui l’a placé sous mandat de dépôt à la prison centrale de Libreville.

items.title: Mali: Clément Dembélé, innocenté mais emprisonné depuis trois ans

original_payload.original_title: Mali: Clément Dembélé, innocenté mais emprisonné depuis trois ans
original_payload.original_body:
Mali: Clément Dembélé, innocenté mais emprisonné depuis trois ans
Au Mali, cela fait tout juste trois ans, ce mardi 17 novembre, que Clément Dembélé est en prison. Accusé d'avoir menacé de mort le président de Transition, le général Assimi Goïta, dans un enregistrement ayant circulé sur les réseaux sociaux, le militant anticorruption a rapidement été mis hors de cause par une expertise technique. Un juge a même ordonné sa libération à plusieurs reprises, mais le procureur du très redouté pôle anticybercriminalité s'y est opposé, et la Cour suprême a elle-même rejeté la demande de libération en août. Eduardo Gonzalez est l'expert indépendant mandaté par les Nations unies sur les droits humains au Mali.
Publié le :  17/11/2026 - 04:40
1 min     Temps de lecture
La Maison centrale d'arrêt de Bamako, au Mali  (Image d'illustration)        © MICHELE CATTANIAFP
Par :
David Baché
Publicité
Eduardo Gonzalez, expert indépendant mandaté par les Nations unies sur les droits humains au Mali, l'assure : «  Clément Dembélé est innocent et Clément Dembélé a des droits, consacrés par la Constitution malienne et par le droit international.  »
L'universitaire, privé de liberté depuis trois années, «  est un homme innocent  ». «  C'est un être humain qui a passé trois ans en prison de manière arbitraire et injuste. C'est très brutal,  déplore l'expert onusien.  Cette situation évoque le désespoir. J'imagine la préoccupation de ses amis et de sa famille, et aussi la préoccupation de toutes les personnes au   Mali   dont le cœur bat pour la liberté.  »
À lire aussi  Mali: une expertise blanchit Clément Dembélé, toujours en prison
«  Ce n'est pas seulement Clément Dembélé,  rappelle enfin Eduardo Gonzalez.  Il y a beaucoup d'autres dirigeants politiques ou sociaux  [de la société civile, NDLR]  qui souffrent ou ont souffert de détentions arbitraires. J'ai peur que dans une situation où le gouvernement a démontré sa capacité à supprimer les droits politiques et civils, il n'y a pas les conditions pour une justice indépendante . »
À lire aussi  Mali: que reproche-t-on aux 4 militants passés de la Sécurité d'État à la prison?

items.title: Tinubu has moved Nigeria from reforms to prosperity, says Reps Deputy Speaker

original_payload.original_title: Tinubu has moved Nigeria from reforms to prosperity, says Reps Deputy Speaker
original_payload.original_body:
Politics  Tinubu has moved Nigeria from reforms to prosperity, says Reps Deputy Speaker
By  Nefisetu Yakubu   ·   5 hours ago   ·  3 min read
✓
✓
By Leonard Okachie
The Deputy Speaker of the House of Representatives, Dr Benjamin Kalu, says President Bola Tinubu has moved Nigeria from reforms to prosperity.
Kalu made the declaration at the launch of the Abia All Progressives Congress (APC) presidential campaign in Umuahia on Monday.
He said Tinubu had stabilised the currency and ended the Academic Staff Union of Universities (ASUU) strikes.
According to him, the President also introduced the Nigerian Education Loan Fund (NELFUND) and reformed tax policies to promote fiscal stability
“We have gone from reform to the time of prosperity.
“We have gone from shedding tears to the point of commencing our laughter,” he said, likening the pains of reforms to childbirth.
Kalu thanked Tinubu for establishing the South East Development Commission (SEDC) and tackling insecurity through increased recruitment and funding.
He dismissed claims that APC was weak in Abia, saying the crowd at the campaign launch was mobilised within one week.
“Nobody should convert you to a beggar of 25 per cent,” he said, promising that Abia would deliver 75 per cent of its votes.
He said Abia had 2.3 million registered voters and 162,000 APC members, each expected to mobilise 10 additional voters.
Kalu announced the donation of 100 branded vehicles to publicise Tinubu’s achievements across local government areas.
The Abia APC Chairman, Chief Chijioke Chukwu, said Tinubu had embraced the state like a father through appointments, road projects and federal institutions.
He listed the Umuahia-Ikwuano-Ikot Ekpene Road, Omenuko Bridge and Port Harcourt Road among key projects.
Chukwu also appealed to the President to appoint a minister from Abia.
Kalu, who is also Deputy Director-General of the South East II Presidential Campaign Council, assured that Abia would deliver 90 per cent of its votes. He declared that “Abia is APC”.
The APC governorship candidate, Dr Eric Opah, said Abia had demonstrated the party’s dominance and would reward Tinubu with massive votes on Jan. 16, 2027.
The Managing Director of SEDC, Mark Okoye, said Tinubu had broken a 55-year jinx by establishing the commission and approving the South-East 2050 Vision.
In an interview, Dr Lilian Obenwa, President and Founder of Issachar Women of Issachar for Tinubu 2027, pledged grassroots mobilisation.
She said her group would mobilise women through markets and churches to support Tinubu.
The News Agency of Nigeria (NAN) reports that other stakeholders highlighted Tinubu’s administration’s achievements in the South-East and urged residents to re-elect him in 2027.
NAN further reports that the main presidential campaign rally for Tinubu is scheduled for Dec. 7 in Aba. (NAN)

items.title: Link education with practical skills for economic growth, says expert

original_payload.original_title: Link education with practical skills for economic growth, says expert
original_payload.original_body:
Economy/Business  Link education with practical skills for economic growth, says expert
By  Nefisetu Yakubu   ·   32 minutes ago   ·  3 min read
✓
✓
By Vivian Emoni
An expert in the education sector, Mr Samuel Ola, has urged Nigeria to strengthen practical skills training and industry collaboration to improve employability, entrepreneurship and economic development.
Ola made the call in an interview with the News Agency of Nigeria (NAN) on Monday in Abuja.
He said aligning education with industry needs and vocational training would equip young Nigerians with relevant skills for employment and entrepreneurship.
According to him, Nigeria must move beyond certificate-based education to practical skills development to address unemployment and improve economic productivity.
“Stronger collaboration between educational equip Nigerians with practical skills for economic development.
“Education must go beyond classroom instruction and certificates to prepare individuals for employment, entrepreneurship and national development,” he said.
Ola noted that the growing unemployment rate and changing workplace demands made it necessary to align education with practical realities and industry requirements.
According to him, employers continue to face challenges finding graduates with the practical competencies required to perform effectively.
He emphasised the need for stronger partnerships among educators, training institutions, employers, government and the organised private sector.
The educationist said education should provide a foundation, while practical exposure, technical competence and entrepreneurial thinking would help translate knowledge into productive capacity.
He noted that Nigeria’s young population needed skills that would enable them to secure employment, identify opportunities and establish sustainable businesses.
He described the growing attention to Technical and Vocational Education and Training (TVET) as timely in addressing unemployment and skills gaps.
The expert cited the Federal Government’s Innovation Development and Effectiveness in the Acquisition of Skills (IDEAS-TVET) programme as an example of efforts to strengthen practical skills development among young Nigerians.
He said 777 young Nigerians were undergoing training under the programme’s third cohort in the Federal Capital Territory (FCT).
According to him, the beneficiaries are receiving training across seven Training Service Providers on digital and creative media, beauty, construction and agriculture.
He said the initiative, supported by the World Bank would improve beneficiaries’ opportunities for employment, freelancing and entrepreneurship.
He emphasised the importance of mentorship, access to equipment, industry exposure, internships and continuous professional development in skills acquisition.
The educationist urged educators to embrace innovation, digital transformation and industry partnerships to make learning more relevant to changing economic demands.
He also called on the private sector to recognise educators as strategic partners in human capital development and practical skills training.
According to him, the Chambers of Commerce and Industry can facilitate partnerships between businesses and training institutions, identify industry skills gaps and promote enterprise development.
He added that skills development programmes should provide trainees with mentorship, professional networks and opportunities to translate their competencies into economic value.
Ola said that Nigeria’s educational progress should be measured by workforce productivity, enterprise growth and the ability of citizens to contribute meaningfully to national development. (NAN)

items.title: Group advocates early teaching of tolerance to promote national unity

original_payload.original_title: Group advocates early teaching of tolerance to promote national unity
original_payload.original_body:
General News  Group advocates early teaching of tolerance to promote national unity
By  Funmilayo Adeyemi   ·   55 minutes ago   ·  4 min read
✓
✓
By Sumaila Ogbaje/Stephen Benjamin
The National Festival of Tolerance and Peaceful Coexistence Programme has advocated the early teaching of lawful tolerance to Nigerian children to promote national unity and peaceful coexistence.
The National Coordinator of the programme, Ijeoma Akwara, made the call on Monday at an event to commemorate the 2026 International Day for Tolerance at Model Primary School, Apo Legislative Quarters, Abuja.
The event, themed “Lawful Tolerance”, featured the distribution of the second edition of the Lawful Tolerance storybook to pupils in Primary 5 and 6.
Akwara said the initiative was designed to educate children on the importance of respecting cultural, religious and ethnic differences while upholding the rule of law.
She explained that Nigeria, as a member state of UNESCO and a signatory to the 1995 Declaration of Principles on Tolerance, had a responsibility to promote mutual understanding and peaceful coexistence among its diverse population.
According to her, the declaration encourages people of different ethnicities, ideologies, religions and social backgrounds to accept their differences and live together peacefully.
“Lawful tolerance is just saying the same thing. It is a simple concept that makes you understand that tolerance is not oppression, but love for culture, which means respecting, appreciating and understanding each other within the boundaries of the law,” she said.
Akwara said the school initiative was one of about six components of the National Festival of Tolerance and Peaceful Coexistence Programme.
She explained that the component, known as “Adapted School: Read to Me Today”, involved adopting schools and educating pupils on values such as tolerance, mutual respect and peaceful coexistence.
“We started with schools because we believe that it is important for our children to celebrate a wonderful ideology, which is the ability to be each other’s neighbour, irrespective of tribe, religion or status.
“We want to catch them young. They are all from different places and go back to different homes. It is important that the children are carried along while we prepare for the adults,” she said.
The coordinator said the programme would also organise an academic symposium in December to examine ways of promoting lawful tolerance, from the classroom to the wider society.
She called on individuals and organisations to support the initiative by adopting schools and ensuring that every child had access to a copy of the storybook.
Earlier, Mr Ojo Michael, representing the Nigerian National Commission for UNESCO (NACOM-UNESCO), said the International Day for Tolerance was established in 1995 to address divisions arising from differences in religion, language, culture and other aspects of human identity.
He said the annual commemoration was aimed at encouraging people across nations and communities to recognise their shared humanity and embrace peaceful coexistence despite their differences.
Ojo said the choice of the school for the event was deliberate, given its diverse population of pupils from different states, ethnic groups and religious backgrounds.
“When you see any school in this country, it constitutes Nigerians. They are not all from the same state or religion. They come from the East, West, North and South,” he said.
He said educating children on tolerance would help them become ambassadors of peace and contribute to building a more united Nigeria.
“We are doing this in order to preach peace into the lives of our children, who are the greater tomorrow, so that they can learn to live in peace and become peace ambassadors in our country,” he said.
Ojo also urged political leaders to demonstrate commitment to peaceful coexistence by fulfilling promises made to Nigerians during election campaigns.
He stressed that promoting peace required commitment from both citizens and political leaders entrusted with the responsibility of governance. (NAN)
Edited by Isaac Aregbesola

items.title: FG unveils A-Z scorecard to showcase education reforms, mobilise grassroots support

original_payload.original_title: FG unveils A-Z scorecard to showcase education reforms, mobilise grassroots support
original_payload.original_body:
Metro  FG unveils A-Z scorecard to showcase education reforms, mobilise grassroots support
By  Funmilayo Adeyemi   ·   55 minutes ago   ·  4 min read
✓
✓
By Hayatullah ​‌⁠⁠‌‌‍⁠⁠‍‍‍​‌⁠‌‍‌‌​Idris
The Federal Government has unveiled the Renewed Hope Education A–Z Scorecard to showcase its achievements and communicate ongoing reforms in the education sector to Nigerians at the grassroots.
The Minister of Education, Dr Tunji Alausa, unveiled the scorecard on Monday in Abuja, describing it as a resource designed to provide information on the administration’s achievements and enable grassroots mobilisers to communicate its interventions to citizens.
Alausa said the initiative was aimed at making information on the administration’s education sector renewal efforts accessible to Nigerians, particularly during the ongoing political mobilisation ahead of the 2027 general elections.
He said the scorecard documented 26 components of the government’s education interventions, covering different levels of the education system, from foundational education to tertiary institutions.
According to him, the interventions address critical areas such as access to education, teacher development, technical and vocational education, student financing, digital learning and the reduction of out-of-school children.
The minister identified some of the initiatives captured in the scorecard to include the improved agreement with the Academic Staff Union of Universities (ASUU), Better Education Service Delivery for All (BESDA), Campus Mobility Initiative, Diaspora BRIDGE and Empowering Educators.
Others are Free Technical Education, Girl-Child Education, HOPE Education, Inspire Live!, Joint Admissions and Matriculation Board (JAMB) admissions reform, medical education expansion, Nigerian Education Loan Fund (NELFUND), and interventions targeting out-of-school children.
The scorecard also features the Student Venture Capital Grant, Technical and Vocational Education and Training (TVET), and expanded digital access, among other interventions.
Alausa said the scorecard would be made available in both hard and soft copies to enable campaign mobilisers and other stakeholders to access and share information about the government’s achievements.
He disclosed that the electronic version was available on a dedicated website created by the ministry.
The minister urged members of the Presidential Campaign Council and other stakeholders to take the information to communities, wards and polling units rather than limiting the communication of government achievements to Abuja.
He said the education sector had recorded interventions across primary, secondary and tertiary education, adding that the scorecard would help Nigerians understand the practical outcomes of the administration’s policies.
Alausa also called on other ministers to make similar presentations of their respective sectors’ achievements to equip grassroots mobilisers with relevant information.
Earlier, the Minister of State for Education, Dr Suwaiba Sa’idu Ahmed, said the scorecard brought together the administration’s education policies, programmes and achievements in an accessible format to support community engagement.
Ahmed said the document was also translated into Hausa, Igbo and Yoruba to ensure that Nigerians could understand the government’s interventions in languages familiar to them.
She explained that the initiative was designed to connect government policies with the everyday concerns of families, students and teachers.
According to her, the scorecard provides information that can help parents understand available opportunities to keep their children in school, young people access skills development programmes and teachers identify available support for improved teaching.
She cited the EduRevamp initiative as one of the interventions supporting teachers.
Ahmed urged grassroots mobilisers to use the scorecard alongside other evidence of the administration’s efforts to engage communities and communicate available opportunities.
In her opening remarks, Hadiza Usman, Assistant Secretary of the All Progressives Congress (APC) Presidential Campaign Council, said the unveiling brought together two important responsibilities of leadership: delivering on commitments and accounting for their implementation.
Usman said education remained central to President Bola Tinubu’s development agenda, noting that sustainable economic growth, industrialisation, technological advancement and social progress depended on deliberate investment in human capital.
She described the education A–Z Scorecard as an instrument of transparency, public engagement and accountability rather than merely a record of achievements.
Usman identified the Nigerian Education Sector Renewal Initiative, the Digital Opportunities for Transformation (DOT) framework, NELFUND and investments in technical and vocational education as some of the interventions supporting reforms in the sector.
She stressed that the success of education policies should be measured by their impact on people’s lives, including children returning to school, young women completing their education, students accessing higher education despite financial challenges and teachers receiving better support.
The APC official urged stakeholders to take the administration’s achievements to communities across the country, saying Nigerians deserved to know what the government had promised and what it had delivered.
She added that the next phase of the Renewed Hope Agenda would focus on continuity, consolidation and expansion of interventions that had demonstrated results, while deepening reforms and strengthening institutions.
The event brought together officials of the Federal Ministry of Education, members of the Presidential Campaign Council and other stakeholders in the education sector. (NAN) nannews.ng

items.title: Stories of survival and pain: Children amid Israel’s war on south Lebanon

original_payload.original_title: Stories of survival and pain: Children amid Israel’s war on south Lebanon
original_payload.original_body:
Kfar Reman, Lebanon –  It was the morning of September 7 when we arrived at the site of an Israeli attack in the village of Kfar Reman in southern Lebanon. Bulldozers were digging through the rubble of a home destroyed in an overnight air strike, searching for the bodies of two children.
Ten members of the same family, spanning three generations, had already been found in the building’s collapsed rooms, among them two survivors.
Recommended Stories

list 2 of 3  Flames engulf Syrian refugee camp in eastern Lebanon
list 3 of 3  Israeli drone filmed flying low outside homes in southern Lebanon
end of list
Two months later, I met 10-year-old Zainab and her eight-year-old brother Mustafa. After losing their parents and elder sister, Fatima, and their one-month-old brother, Ahmed, they now live with their grandmother. Both were thrown out of the house due to the intensity of the blast, but their physical wounds were no longer visible.
Zainab had a constant smile, but she was hiding sadness which she did not know how to express in words.
Mustafa was different. There was no smile. He is angry at Israel. When I asked him to share his story or a message to the world instead of speaking to me, he looked straight at the camera.
“What they did is they took my home and my parents from me,” Mustafa said. He paused for a few seconds and continued, “Because of them I no longer live in peace.”
Children in Lebanon have been badly affected by Israel’s attacks on the country [Screengrab/Al Jazeera]   More than a thousand children were injured in Israeli attacks between March and August this year, according to the United Nations.
Some lost a parent or both their parents while more than 260 were killed. That figure represents an average of seven children killed or injured every day over those six months – nearly double the number at the start of the latest on-again, off-again conflict between Hezbollah and Israel in late 2023.

Thousands of US customers reported problems accessing online banking services after JPMorgan Chase said a software issue caused knock-on effects for transactions involving other banks.

items.title: US moves to block China’s remote access to AI chips amid Nvidia scandal

original_payload.original_title: US moves to block China’s remote access to AI chips amid Nvidia scandal
original_payload.original_body:
United States President Donald Trump’s administration has announced new restrictions on China’s access to advanced chips amid fallout from the alleged spy scandal involving AI giant Nvidia.
The rule announced by the Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) on Monday aims to prevent Chinese AI developers from getting around export controls by remotely accessing data centres in third countries, particularly in Southeast Asia.
Recommended Stories
list of 4 items    list 1 of 4  EU agrees to resurrect cooperation deal with Syria
list 2 of 4  Trump departs for ASEAN on summit with Xi and Putin
list 3 of 4  Paraguay ex-president moved to military jail amid special treatment reports
list 4 of 4  Ethiopia Moyale clashes disrupt livelihoods as territorial dispute deepens
end of list
It designates Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand and Brazil as countries with an “unacceptable risk of diversion” and requires anyone seeking to ship advanced chips to those destinations to obtain an export licence.
BIS, which sits under the Department of Commerce, said the change was a “logical extension” of the existing requirement for companies to obtain a licence to export or transfer chips to firms based in China.
“The United States is the global leader in advanced computing and super intelligence technology and is committed to promoting the global adoption of American technology for legitimate commercial purposes while ensuring that sensitive technologies are not exploited in ways that threaten US national security,” BIS said in a statement.
While Chinese firms are barred from importing the most advanced graphics processing units (GPUs) under US export controls, they had until now been legally able to take advantage of remote access to top-of-the-line computing power at data centres in countries such as Singapore, Malaysia and Thailand.
Singapore, which hosts dozens of data centres, said on Tuesday that it was “studying the details of this new measure carefully”.

items.title: Diabète et maladies non transmissibles : le Programme national de lutte lance une campagne gratuite de dépistage à N’Djamena

original_payload.original_title: Diabète et maladies non transmissibles : le Programme national de lutte lance une campagne gratuite de dépistage à N’Djamena
original_payload.original_body:
À l’occasion de la Journée mondiale de lutte contre le diabète, le Programme national de lutte contre le diabète et les maladies non transmissibles, en collaboration avec la Société tchadienne d’endocrinologie, des maladies métaboliques et de nutrition, a lancé, ce lundi 16 novembre 2026, une campagne gratuite de dépistage du diabète et de l’hypertension artérielle à l’hôpital Mère et Enfant de Toukra. Prévue pour cinq jours, cette opération vise à favoriser le diagnostic précoce et à rapprocher les services de santé des populations.
La campagne intervient dans un contexte de progression des maladies non transmissibles au Tchad. Selon la coordinatrice du Programme national de lutte contre le diabète et les maladies non transmissibles, Dr Habiba Abdoulaye Affadine, qui s’appuie sur des chiffres de la Fédération internationale du diabète, la prévalence du diabète était estimée à 7 % en 2024.
Elle souligne que le pays fait face à plusieurs défis, notamment le diagnostic tardif, l’insuffisance de ressources humaines spécialisées et les difficultés d’accès à des soins de qualité.
« Les complications liées au diabète constituent une cause importante de morbidité et de mortalité », a-t-elle rappelé. Pour répondre à cette situation, le projet Sanofi GHU by SE accompagne les efforts de renforcement du système de santé, notamment à travers la formation des professionnels de santé, la numérisation des services de prise en charge et la mobilisation des acteurs du secteur privé.
La campagne de dépistage s’inscrit dans cette dynamique. Elle constitue également la première édition de la caravane dénommée « 3.0 Santé Tchad », dont l’une des nouveautés est l’enrôlement biométrique des patients. Selon la coordinatrice, les activités sont prévues dans plusieurs sites de la capitale, notamment dans les 1er, 6e, 7e et 9e arrondissements.
Lire aussi:  Prévention du diabète : les conseils du nutritionniste Yanwe Vincent Delsikreo
Présent à la cérémonie, le médecin-chef du district sanitaire du 9e arrondissement, Dr Baroua Haroun Seid, a salué l’initiative et invité les populations à profiter de cette occasion pour connaître leur état de santé. « Le dépistage n’est pas une peur, mais une sagesse. Une personne qui vient de se faire dépister s’informe et prend de l’avance sur sa situation sanitaire », a-t-il déclaré.
Pour la maire adjointe du 9e arrondissement, Fatimé Kossan Allatchi, cette caravane constitue une réponse concrète aux défis sanitaires auxquels les populations sont confrontées.
Lire aussi :  Santé : le cri du cœur de Kindi Véronique, qui combat le diabète depuis 11 ans
Elle estime que le diabète et les maladies cardiovasculaires progressent dans la communauté et sont souvent diagnostiqués tardivement. « Grâce à cette caravane de dépistage, nous pourrons sauver beaucoup de vies », a-t-elle affirmé, tout en assurant le soutien de la commune à cette initiative.
Au-delà du dépistage, les organisateurs entendent renforcer la sensibilisation et encourager les populations à adopter une démarche préventive face aux maladies non transmissibles.
La campagne, qui se poursuit jusqu’au 20 novembre, offre ainsi aux habitants concernés une occasion de se faire dépister gratuitement et de bénéficier d’une meilleure orientation sanitaire.

items.title: Apple to face trial over alleged iPhone repair restrictions in France

original_payload.original_title: Apple to face trial over alleged iPhone repair restrictions in France
original_payload.original_body:
Apple is to stand trial in Paris in June 2027 on suspicion of having organised the planned obsolescence of various iPhone models by preventing repairs outside official outlets, a source close to the case told AFP on Tuesday.
The case brought by French prosecutors against the US tech giant on charges of “obstructing repair and refurbishment” is a first, campaign group Stop Planned Obsolescence said, welcoming the move after filing a complaint on December 7, 2022.
“We strongly contest these unfounded allegations,” Apple said when contacted by AFP.
Planned obsolescence refers to techniques used by manufacturers to deliberately shorten the lifespan of their products, generally electronic devices, thereby encouraging consumers to discard and replace them more frequently.

original_payload.original_title: US to close AI chip loophole after Nvidia scandal
original_payload.original_body:
The United States announced tougher export controls on AI chips on Monday after a scandal involving Nvidia co-founder Jensen Huang exposed a loophole allegedly exploited by Chinese companies.
The news came the day before Californian chip titan Nvidia reports its first earnings since Huang’s departure as CEO, with investors questioning if the artificial intelligence boom can hold strong.
Under Washington’s new rules, data centres anywhere in the world will need a US license to provide large volumes of computing power from advanced chips to companies headquartered in China, Macau or other countries under US arms embargoes.
The rules also require licenses to ship advanced chips to Singapore, Malaysia, Thailand, Indonesia and Brazil, countries the US Commerce Department says present a “higher-than-normal risk of diversion” of the chips.

Les Black Stars totalisent six points après leur deuxième succès contre la Somalie. La Gambie, qui compte un match de moins, reçoit mardi la Côte d’Ivoire.

Le Ghana a rejoint la Gambie à six points dans le groupe C des éliminatoires de la CAN 2027 après sa victoire 1-0 contre la Somalie, lundi 16 novembre à Sekondi-Takoradi. Les Gambiens, qui comptent un match de moins, accueillent ce mardi la Côte d’Ivoire, leader avec neuf points.
Jordan Ayew a inscrit l’unique but sur penalty à la 36e minute. Le capitaine ghanéen avait manqué une tentative lors de la  première confrontation, remportée 2-0 par les Black Stars  le 12 novembre. Après deux défaites lors des premières journées, le Ghana a ainsi pris les six points possibles face à la Somalie.
Les Ghanéens ont désormais disputé quatre rencontres, contre trois pour la Gambie et la Côte d’Ivoire. Ils occupent la troisième place de leur groupe et devront attendre les deux dernières journées, en mars 2027, pour poursuivre leur campagne. Les deux premières places donnent accès à la phase finale.
Le duel entre la Gambie et la Côte d’Ivoire se disputera mardi 17 novembre à 16 h GMT, soit 17 h à Cotonou. Vainqueurs 2-1 du match aller à Bouaké, les Éléphants obtiendraient leur qualification en cas de nouveau succès. Ils comptent trois victoires en trois matchs.
Une victoire de la Gambie porterait les Scorpions à neuf points, trois de plus que le Ghana. En cas de défaite, ils resteraient à six points avant les deux dernières journées. La Somalie, battue à quatre reprises et toujours sans point, est déjà éliminée.
La CAN 2027 se déroulera du 19 juin au 17 juillet au Kenya, en Tanzanie et en Ouganda. Les cinquième et sixième journées des éliminatoires sont prévues entre le 22 et le 30 mars 2027.

Le Nigeria reçoit la République démocratique du Congo mardi 17 novembre à Ikenne avec deux buts de retard et l’obligation de renverser le score de l’aller pour poursuivre sa campagne de qualification à la CAN des moins de 23 ans 2027. Prévue au Remo Stars Stadium, la rencontre commencera à 15 h GMT, soit 16 h à Cotonou.
Les Olympic Eagles se sont inclinés 2-0 vendredi à Lubumbashi. Pour passer devant au score cumulé après le temps réglementaire, ils devront gagner par au moins trois buts d’écart. Une victoire nigériane 2-0 rétablirait l’égalité sur les deux manches.
Les Congolais ont pris leur avance avant la pause. Le défenseur nigérian Samuel Friday James a marqué contre son camp, puis Filozofe Mabete a doublé la mise. Les  deux buts inscrits à Lubumbashi  obligent désormais les Nigérians à attaquer tout en évitant d’aggraver leur retard.
La RDC avait dû franchir le premier tour en éliminant la Mauritanie, tandis que le Nigeria était directement entré dans la compétition au deuxième tour. Avant cette double confrontation, la fédération nigériane avait retenu un groupe de 23 joueurs comprenant notamment le milieu Daniel Daga, le gardien Michael Atata et l’attaquant Abdulmuiz Adeleke.
Le vainqueur accédera au troisième et dernier tour, programmé en mars 2027. Sept confrontations aller-retour désigneront alors les équipes qui rejoindront l’Égypte, pays organisateur, en phase finale de la CAN U23.
Le tournoi constituera également une étape de la qualification africaine au football masculin des Jeux olympiques de Los Angeles 2028. Champion olympique en 1996 et médaillé de bronze en 2016, le Nigeria a manqué les éditions de Tokyo et de Paris.

Au Sénégal, les moyens proposés pour la Justice progressent, mais les députés contestent leur répartition et le cadrage des finances publiques.
Économie      Par  Christian Mbeumo
·   17 Nov. 2026 à 05:36  17/11/26 05:36       ·   2 min  de lecture

L’Assemblée nationale du Sénégal à Dakar, le 28 septembre 2012 (archives). Photo : Lamine Niang / Photowalk, CC BY-SA 3.0 (format adapté).
Partager
Ajouter Bénin Web TV à vos sources préférées
SOMMAIRE
Des crédits réduits pour l’administration pénitentiaire
Lire en :
English (World)
La Commission des finances et du contrôle budgétaire de l’Assemblée nationale du Sénégal a rejeté, vendredi 13 novembre 2026, le projet de budget du ministère de la Justice pour 2027. Le garde des Sceaux, Moussa Sarr, a défendu ses crédits devant les députés réunis en commission élargie à celle des lois, sans obtenir leur approbation.
Le département sollicite 85,76 milliards de FCFA en crédits de paiement, pour 93,25 milliards de FCFA en autorisations d’engagement. Les crédits de paiement augmentent de 5,03 milliards par rapport aux 80,73 milliards inscrits en 2026, soit une progression de 6,2 %. Cette hausse globale s’accompagne toutefois de diminutions dans certains programmes.
Les parlementaires ont contesté la baisse des moyens pénitentiaires et soulevé des questions sur les fouilles corporelles, le recours aux mandats de dépôt et les différences de tarifs du casier judiciaire entre tribunaux. Des commissaires ont également critiqué la sincérité du cadrage budgétaire et la transmission tardive de documents, alors que le projet de loi de finances rectificative pour 2026 a déjà été rejeté.
Des crédits réduits pour l’administration pénitentiaire
L’administration pénitentiaire devait recevoir 29,24 milliards de FCFA en 2027, soit une diminution de 5,4 % sur un an. Cette enveloppe prévisionnelle comprend 6,27 milliards pour l’alimentation des détenus et 1,14 milliard pour leur prise en charge sanitaire. La diminution des crédits de ce programme a figuré parmi les points discutés par les députés.
À l’inverse, les moyens destinés à la justice judiciaire atteignent 32,54 milliards de FCFA, en hausse de 24,3 %. La protection judiciaire de l’enfant bénéficie de 9,22 milliards, soit 13,2 % de plus qu’en 2026. Les crédits consacrés à la bonne gouvernance et aux droits humains s’établissent à 1,12 milliard, en progression de 47,6 %.
La numérisation des procédures judiciaires doit recevoir 1,15 milliard de FCFA en 2027, dans le cadre d’un programme évalué à 10,7 milliards sur la période 2025-2029. La plateforme eJustice a commencé à dématérialiser certaines procédures dans des juridictions pilotes le 10 septembre. Devant les parlementaires, Moussa Sarr a déclaré que « le ministère de la Justice a besoin de davantage de moyens ».
Le vote défavorable est intervenu au stade de la commission, avant l’examen du texte en séance plénière. L’Assemblée nationale doit reprendre l’étude du  projet de loi de finances 2027  mercredi 18 novembre à partir de 10 heures.

Andy Robertson est devenu lundi 16 novembre le joueur le plus sélectionné de l’histoire de l’équipe masculine d’Écosse en disputant son 103e match international contre la Suisse. Le capitaine de 32 ans a établi ce record à Saint-Gall, au cours d’une soirée qui s’est terminée par une défaite 4-0 lors de la dernière journée de la Ligue des nations.
Le latéral écossais dépasse Kenny Dalglish, dont la marque de 102 sélections entre 1971 et 1986 tenait depuis quarante ans. Robertson avait fait ses débuts internationaux en 2014, face à la Pologne. Il avait égalé le total de son illustre prédécesseur avant ce déplacement en Suisse.
Sur le terrain, la Suisse a pris l’avantage à la 22e minute, lorsque Lewis Ferguson a détourné le ballon dans son propre but. Les Écossais, qui avaient obtenu des situations dangereuses en première période, ont également perdu Aaron Hickey sur blessure avant la pause.
Le match a définitivement basculé dès le retour des vestiaires. Winsley Boteli a doublé la mise à la 47e minute, puis Alvyn Sanches a marqué quatre minutes plus tard. Zeki Amdouni a inscrit le quatrième but suisse à la 89e minute, portant à quatre le nombre de buts concédés par le gardien Angus Gunn.
L’Écosse termine ainsi troisième du groupe B1 avec sept points en six rencontres. Elle restera en Ligue B et manquera les barrages de promotion. La Suisse finit première du groupe, tandis que la Slovénie a pris la deuxième place grâce à sa victoire 3-0 en Macédoine du Nord. Les Écossais n’ont gagné que deux matchs dans cette campagne, tous deux face à la Macédoine du Nord.

original_payload.original_title: Guerre en Ukraine : Trump évoque 25000 soldats tués chaque mois dans les deux camps
original_payload.original_body:
Photo : DR
Guerre en Ukraine : Trump évoque 25000 soldats tués chaque mois dans les deux camps
16/11/2026    par    Amos Traoré
Facebook  Twitter  WhatsApp
Ce lundi 16 novembre, au cours d’un point de presse avec des journalistes à la  Maison-Blanche , le président américain  Donald Trump  a évoqué l’ampleur des pertes humaines provoquées par la guerre en  Ukraine . Le locataire de la Maison-Blanche affirme que les forces russes et ukrainiennes perdent environ  25000 soldats  chaque mois.
Interrogé sur les dossiers qu’il compte aborder lors de sa prochaine rencontre avec  Vladimir Poutine et Xi Jinping , le magnat de l’immobilier a insisté sur la nécessité de mettre fin au conflit russo-ukrainien.  « L’Ukraine et la Russie perdent 25000 soldats par mois » , a déclaré Donald Trump devant les journalistes.
Trump va t-il faire bouger les lignes ?
Par cette estimation, le 47e président des USA fait référence aux pertes enregistrées par les deux armées réunies, sans avancer de chiffres distincts pour  Moscou et Kiev .  Rappelons que le 9 novembre dernier, Trump avait déjà affirmé que la Russie et l’Ukraine perdaient en moyenne 25000 personnes par mois, en grande majorité des militaires. Il avait alors évoqué un bilan de 32000 personnes pour le mois d’octobre. Le milliardaire américain avait insisté sur les conséquences humaines de ce conflit complexe qui s’est enlisé.
Les USA poursuivent les négociations diplomatiques autour du conflit entre la Russie et l’Ukraine afin de trouver des consensus qui vont permettre de déboucher sur des pistes de sorties de crise. Le prochain sommet entre Donald Trump, Vladimir Poutine et Xi Jinping doit permettre entre autres d’aborder la situation en Ukraine. Le locataire de la Maison-Blanche entend discuter de ce dossier avec Vladimir Poutine et Xi Jinping, dans l’optique de faire avancer les échanges sur une issue à la guerre.
